cards.t: The four immunopathologies (allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, cancer)
q: what are the four immunopathologies
which immune disorders are overreactions and which are underreactions
how is cancer related to the immune system
cards.x:
The immune system can go wrong in four main ways. They sort neatly into overreaction and underreaction. The overreactions are allergy and autoimmunity. Allergy (hypersensitivity) is an exaggerated, misdirected response to an allergen that uses the same machinery as normal protective immunity. Autoimmunity is an abnormal response to the body's own antigens, which is typically an overreaction. The underreactions are immunodeficiency, where immunity is missing or lost, and cancer.

Cancer is the odd one because it is both a cause and an effect of immune dysfunction. Immune surveillance normally keeps cancer in check, so when immunity fails a tumor can slip through. Once established, a successful tumor evades and actively manipulates the response, suppressing immunity even further. Allergy itself then splits into four types. Types I, II and III are driven by B cells (antibody), while IV is driven by T cells.

cards.t: The four types of hypersensitivity compared
k: type I II III IV hypersensitivity
q: what are the four types of hypersensitivity
how do the hypersensitivity types differ
which hypersensitivity types are antibody mediated
cards.x:
The four hypersensitivity types are defined by the effector mechanism, meaning what actually does the damage.
- Type I (immediate): immunoglobulin E stuck to the surface of cells is crosslinked by allergen, and mast cells, basophils and eosinophils release inflammatory mediators. Hay fever, hives, anaphylactic shock.
- Type II: immunoglobulin G or M binds antigens on a cell's surface, complement is activated, and the cell is lysed (burst) by the membrane attack complex or eaten by phagocytes. Transfusion reactions.
- Type III: immunoglobulin G or M binds soluble antigens, and the immune complexes embed in basement membranes and start inflammation. Serum sickness, lupus.
- Type IV (delayed): T cells, not antibody, destroy tissue. Contact dermatitis.

So types I to III are antibody (B cell) driven and type IV is T cell driven.

cards.t: Mast cells, eosinophils and basophils
k: cells in allergy and parasite defense
q: what do mast cells do
what is the role of eosinophils and basophils
which cells are involved in allergy and parasite defense
cards.x:
Mast cells, eosinophils and basophils are the cells that defend against parasites and also drive allergy, because allergy borrows the same toolkit.
- Mast cells sit on epithelial surfaces (the body's linings). They carry immunoglobulin E on their surface and are filled with granules of cytokines, ready to be dumped out.
- Eosinophils are granulocytes that release toxic mediators in an immunoglobulin E response. They are aimed at eukaryotic parasites.
- Basophils are rare granulocytes. They start a type 2 helper T cell response and the production of immunoglobulin E, and they go with helminths (parasitic worms).

Allergy uses this toolkit because many allergens resemble parasite antigens. So the body treats a harmless pollen grain with a response designed for a worm.

cards.t: How a type I allergic reaction happens (two doses)
q: how does a type 1 allergic reaction work
why doesn't the first exposure to an allergen cause symptoms
what is mast cell degranulation
cards.x:
A type I allergy takes two exposures. The first, the sensitizing dose, generally produces no signs or symptoms: the allergen is carried to a lymph node, specific B cells turn into plasma cells that make immunoglobulin E, and that antibody parks on mast cells and basophils. Each mast cell can bind 10,000 to 40,000 immunoglobulin E molecules, so it ends up loaded like a set trap.

On later contact, the provocative dose, the same allergen binds the immunoglobulin E already sitting on the mast cell and bridges neighboring antibodies. The mast cell degranulates, which means it empties its granules and releases inflammatory cytokines into the blood. That is why symptoms can show up in organs far from where the allergen entered. Allergens are immunogenic proteins, or smaller molecules called haptens, and usually enter through the respiratory tract, gut or skin; the organ that reacts may or may not be the entry point.

cards.t: Skin allergies: hives, angioedema and eczema
q: what causes hives
what is the difference between urticaria and angioedema
what is atopic dermatitis
cards.x:
Three skin conditions come from allergic reactions in the skin, and what separates them is where and how long.
- Urticaria (hives): mast cells in the skin release histamine, causing raised, itchy swelling.
- Angio-edema: the same idea, but mast cells deeper in the skin are activated, so the swelling lies deeper.
- Atopic dermatitis (eczema): a more prolonged allergic response in the skin rather than a quick burst.

The skin is one of the general targets of a type I reaction. The others are the upper respiratory tract, the gastrointestinal tract and the conjunctiva (the lining of the eye). Together the results are rash, itching, redness, rhinitis (runny nose), sneezing, diarrhea and tears.

cards.t: Hay fever, food allergy and allergic asthma
q: what happens in hay fever
why does a food allergy cause hives
how is allergic asthma related to type IV hypersensitivity
cards.x:
These three show the same allergy playing out in different organs.
- Allergic rhinitis (hay fever): an inhaled allergen triggers histamine, which raises capillary permeability and nasal mucus. Eosinophils are attracted from the blood, release their mediators and are shed into the nasal passage.
- Food allergy: vomiting, diarrhea and urticaria. Local histamine acts on the intestinal lining, vessels and smooth muscle. Hives appear because the antigen enters blood vessels and is carried to the skin.
- Allergic asthma: the acute phase is contraction of bronchial smooth muscle, more mucus and airway obstruction. This can lead to chronic asthma, which is type IV, mediated by cytokines and eosinophil granules.

cards.t: Anaphylaxis (systemic and cutaneous)
q: what is anaphylaxis
why does anaphylaxis drop blood pressure
what is a wheal and flare reaction
cards.x:
Anaphylaxis is the extreme version of a type I reaction: a sudden disruption of breathing and circulation that can be fatal in minutes. The allergen reaches the bloodstream. Examples are a bee sting, an antibiotic or serum by injection, or a food such as peanuts by mouth. The allergen activates connective tissue mast cells around blood vessels throughout the body at once. Fluid leaves the blood, so blood pressure drops drastically and tissues swell. Organs are damaged, and constricted airways can cause death by asphyxiation (suffocation). In the United States it causes 500 to 1000 deaths a year.

Cutaneous anaphylaxis is the small, local version: the wheal and flare skin reaction (a raised welt with surrounding redness). It is the reaction used in allergy diagnosis.

cards.t: Why epinephrine reverses anaphylaxis
q: why is epinephrine used in anaphylaxis
how does epinephrine reverse anaphylactic shock
what are the actions of epinephrine in anaphylaxis
cards.x:
Epinephrine is the rescue drug because anaphylaxis collapses blood pressure and constricts the airways at the same moment, and epinephrine reverses both. On a blood pressure curve, pressure collapses at the start of the reaction and climbs back only as the epinephrine level spikes. It works in five ways:
- It stimulates reformation of endothelial tight junctions, the seals between the cells lining blood vessels, so fluid stops leaking out.
- It relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, opening the airways.
- It prevents or decreases swelling (edema) of the upper airway lining.
- It stimulates the heart.
- It binds receptors on immune cells to suppress histamine release.

cards.t: The late phase reaction
q: what is the late phase reaction
why do allergic symptoms come back hours later
how is asthma measured in immediate vs late phase
cards.x:
An immunoglobulin E reaction comes in two waves. The immediate response is the wheal and flare, caused by mast cell degranulation. About 6 hours later comes the late phase reaction, driven by products the cells have to make fresh, such as leukotrienes. It attracts more cells, including eosinophils, whose cytokines enhance the inflammation and make the tissue more sensitive the next time around.

In asthma, the two waves can be measured with forced expiratory volume in 1 second, which is how much air a person can blow out in the first second. The immediate response happens in under 1 hour, and the late phase response comes after more than 6 hours.

cards.t: Type II hypersensitivity (antibody against cell surfaces)
q: what is type 2 hypersensitivity
how does complement destroy cells in type II
what are examples of type II reactions
cards.x:
Type II is the antibody-meets-a-cell reaction. Immunoglobulin G or M binds antigens that sit on the surface of a cell. That stimulates complement. Complement can burst the cell with the membrane attack complex. Phagocytes also eat the antibody-coated cell. The target is a cell, which is the point: the antigen is part of the cell surface.

Examples: transfusion reactions (mismatched blood type), Rh factor disease of the newborn, and some autoimmune diseases. These include autoimmune hemolytic anemia (the body's own red cells are destroyed) and myasthenia gravis (antibodies against acetylcholine receptors).

To tell it from type III: in type II the antibody grabs antigens fixed on a cell; in type III it grabs antigens floating free in the blood.

cards.t: Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex reactions)
q: what is type 3 hypersensitivity
how do immune complexes cause damage
what's an example of a type III reaction
cards.x:
Type III is the immune complex reaction. Immunoglobulin G or M antibodies (sometimes A) grab antigens that are floating free in the blood, not stuck to a cell. The two clump together into immune complexes. It takes a large amount of antigen to make enough of them. The clumps lodge in the basement membranes of epithelial tissues, typically in the joints, skin and kidneys. Complement and phagocytes arrive to clear them, which inflames the tissue around them. So the damage lands wherever the clumps settle, and symptoms are delayed by hours to days. Classic examples are serum sickness (a reaction to foreign animal proteins such as horse serum) and autoimmune conditions such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

A small, local version is the Arthus reaction: inflamed skin blood vessels at the site of a second vaccine injection, which usually settles on its own. Quick way to tell type III from type II: in type II the antibody hits antigens on a cell's surface; in type III it hits antigens floating in the blood.

cards.t: Type IV hypersensitivity (delayed, T cell mediated)
q: what is type 4 hypersensitivity
why is type IV called delayed
what are examples of type IV reactions
cards.x:
Type IV is the delayed reaction, and it is the only one run by T cells rather than antibody. Activated T cells cause the damage, with cytotoxic cells destroying tissue directly.

Examples: infectious allergy to microbes such as tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, histoplasmosis, toxoplasmosis and candidiasis; the tuberculin skin test; contact dermatitis from plants, metals and cosmetics; and graft rejection. Allergic asthma can also become type IV once it turns chronic.

cards.t: Contact dermatitis and why it needs a second exposure
q: what is contact dermatitis
how does contact dermatitis work
why does the rash only show up after the second contact
cards.x:
Contact dermatitis is a skin rash from touching something such as a plant, a metal or a cosmetic. It is a type IV (T cell) reaction. It follows the same two-dose logic as a type I allergy, only with T cells instead of antibody. The first contact is the sensitizing dose, when T cells learn to recognize the substance. Later contact is the reactive dose. The tissue damage comes from cytokines released by macrophages and from cytotoxic T cells.

Poison ivy shows why the first contact causes no quick rash. Its oil binds the skin within about 15 minutes, but making effector T cells takes 7 to 10 days or more. So a first exposure gives at most a delayed rash, and later contacts react much faster. Because it is a T cell reaction, contact dermatitis is tested with a patch test rather than the skin prick used for immunoglobulin E allergies.

cards.t: The hygiene hypothesis
q: what is the hygiene hypothesis
why do parasite infections protect against allergies
cards.x:
The hygiene hypothesis explains why allergies are more common where parasitic worm infections have been wiped out. Many allergens look a lot like parasite antigens. A helminth (worm) infection triggers the same immune profile as allergy: type 2 helper T cell responses, lots of immunoglobulin E, and more eosinophils and mast cells. Yet people with chronic worm infections tend to have less allergic disease, for two proposed reasons.
- The flood of nonspecific immunoglobulin E takes up the receptors on mast cells, basophils and activated eosinophils. That leaves less room for allergen-specific antibody.
- Regulatory T cells keep T cell responses turned down during the long infection.

Remove the worms with better sanitation and treatment, as happened in Western Europe and North America. The idea is that this arm of the immune system is then underused and less well regulated, so it may overreact to harmless things.

cards.t: Who gets allergies: inherited tendency, age and environment
q: are allergies hereditary
can you outgrow an allergy
what affects whether someone develops allergies
cards.x:
A general tendency toward allergy runs in families, but what is passed down is the predisposition, not a specific allergy. A parent's pollen allergy does not guarantee the child gets the same one.

Other things shape the picture too: age, infection and geographic area all matter. Atopic allergies (the inherited, allergy-prone kind) may be lifelong, may be outgrown, or may only appear later in life. The same allergen can also behave differently depending on how a person is exposed to it.

cards.t: Targets of a type I reaction: local versus systemic
k: smooth muscle mucous glands nervous tissue
q: which organs does a type I allergy affect
what are the systemic targets of an allergic reaction
why does an allergy cause changes in blood pressure and breathing
cards.x:
The targets of a type I reaction fall into two groups, general and systemic. The general targets are the skin, upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract and conjunctiva (the lining of the eye). The results are rashes, itching, redness, rhinitis (runny nose), sneezing, diarrhea and tears.

The systemic targets are smooth muscle, mucous glands and nervous tissue. There, blood vessels dilate or constrict, which changes blood pressure and breathing. This is the body-wide pattern that, at its worst, becomes anaphylaxis. Remember too that the organ where the allergy shows may or may not be the place the allergen entered.

cards.t: Diagnosing allergy: skin tests, blood tests, challenge and patch test
q: how is allergy diagnosed
what is a skin prick test
which allergy test is used for contact dermatitis
cards.x:
The first question is whether the patient has an allergy or an infection, since the two can look alike. After that, the test is matched to the problem:
- Skin testing (skin prick, or intradermal, meaning injected into the skin) reads the wheal and flare reaction.
- Blood tests look for specific immunoglobulin E to the suspected allergen; a raised basophil count is not a reliable allergy marker.
- A physician-supervised challenge is used for food allergy when other tests are inconclusive.
- A patch test is used for contact dermatitis, which is type IV.

cards.t: Treating type I hypersensitivity: prevention, drugs and desensitization
q: how is type 1 hypersensitivity managed
what does cromolyn sodium do
which drug blocks leukotrienes in allergy
cards.x:
Type I hypersensitivity is managed three ways: prevention (change the environment and behavior to avoid the allergen), pharmacological control, and desensitization. To remember the drugs, follow the allergy chain from start to finish and note where each one steps in.
- Corticosteroids inhibit lymphocytes, which reduces immunoglobulin E production.
- Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody against immunoglobulin E itself.
- Cromolyn sodium blocks mast cell degranulation.
- Montelukast sodium blocks the action of leukotrienes (the freshly made products behind the late phase reaction).
- Antihistamines bind histamine receptors on the target organs, so histamine has nowhere to land.

Epinephrine sits at the emergency end. It reverses airway constriction and re-establishes endothelial tight junctions.

cards.t: Desensitization (allergen-specific immunotherapy)
q: how does desensitization work for allergies
why do allergy shots help
what is sublingual immunotherapy
cards.x:
Desensitization retrains the immune system by giving the allergen on purpose in small, controlled amounts. The most common form is subcutaneous immunotherapy: small amounts of allergen injected under the skin. The injections stimulate high levels of allergen-specific immunoglobulin G. This blocks the allergen from reaching the immunoglobulin E, so mast cells do not degranulate. It improves reactions in about 80% of the people who complete it.

It is not quite that simple, though. Desensitization also activates regulatory T cells, which inhibit T cell activation of B cells and release anti-inflammatory cytokines. It also induces mediators that damp T cell proliferation and mast cell and eosinophil activity. Sublingual immunotherapy puts the allergen under the tongue as a tablet or liquid. It is used more outside the United States, which has tablets for pollen and dust mite. A 4-year trial of a peanut dose equal to 1/75 of a kernel was effective and safe, protecting against accidental exposure. Similar approaches have worked for kiwi, hazelnut, milk and peach.

cards.t: Transfusion reactions and the cross-match
q: why do transfusion reactions happen
how is a cross-match done
why is the recipient's serum used in the cross-match
cards.x:
A transfusion reaction is a type II reaction. Red blood cells carry ABO (blood type) antigens but no major histocompatibility complex molecules. So ABO is what the immune system sees, and donor and recipient are matched on it. Everyone carries antibodies in their serum against the ABO antigens they lack. That is why blood type O is the universal donor (its cells have no A or B antigen). Type AB (carrying both A and B antigens) is the universal recipient, since its serum has no anti-A or anti-B antibody. Give the wrong blood and those antibodies attack the donor red cells. Complement is activated and the cells lyse, which can be fatal. Even when complement activation is incomplete, the antibody-coated cells are left for natural killer cells and macrophages to destroy. The fallout from red cell destruction is blocked glomeruli (the kidney's filters), fever and jaundice.

The cross-match mixes the recipient's serum with the donor's red cells, not the other way around. Even whole blood carries too little donor antibody to coat the recipient's cells densely enough to react.

cards.t: Rh factor and hemolytic disease of the newborn
q: what is hemolytic disease of the newborn
why is the first Rh incompatible pregnancy usually fine
when is Rhogam given
cards.x:
Rh disease is a type II reaction that can happen when an Rh-negative mother who has been sensitized carries an Rh-positive baby. The Rh antigen is found only on Rh-positive cells. An Rh-negative person makes no anti-Rh antibody unless she has been sensitized, either by a bad transfusion or by an incompatible pregnancy. That is why the first pregnancy is normally fine: it is the pregnancy that sensitizes her. Later pregnancies may be hemolytic, meaning her antibodies destroy the baby's red cells (hemolytic disease of the newborn, also called erythroblastosis fetalis). Immunoglobulin G is the only antibody that crosses the placenta, which is why a sensitized mother's next Rh-positive baby is the one at risk.

Prevention is passive immunization. That means giving ready-made antibody against the Rh antigen (Rhogam) so the mother never becomes sensitized. It is given at 26 to 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth, and after prenatal invasive tests, abdominal injury or accidental exposure.

cards.t: Types of grafts (autograft, isograft, allograft, xenograft)
q: what is the difference between an allograft and a xenograft
what is an isograft
what controls graft rejection
cards.x:
Grafts are named by where the tissue came from.
- Autograft: from the patient's own body, such as a skin, gum or vein graft.
- Isograft: from a genetically identical twin.
- Allograft: from another member of the same species.
- Xenograft: from another species.

Rejection runs both ways: the host may reject the graft, and the graft may reject the host. The major histocompatibility complex governs it, since how well different grafts succeed depends on how compatible these molecules are between donor and recipient.

cards.t: Types of graft rejection and their hypersensitivity type
q: what are the types of transplant rejection
which hypersensitivity type causes hyperacute rejection
why does chronic rejection happen
cards.x:
Graft rejection comes in four forms, and each one maps onto a hypersensitivity type (none of them is type I).
- Hyperacute rejection (type II): the recipient already has antibody against the graft's antigens. The graft becomes engorged and purple from hemorrhage and fails.
- Acute rejection (type IV): effector T cells respond to differences in human leukocyte antigens between donor and recipient.
- Chronic rejection (type III): months or years later, immune complexes in the graft's vessel walls thicken them until the blood supply fails. It causes failure of more than half of kidney and heart transplants after 10 years or more.
- Graft versus host disease (type IV): donor cells attack host tissue.

cards.t: How acute rejection works (the graft's dendritic cells)
q: how does acute rejection happen
why is acute rejection type IV and not type II
what role do dendritic cells play in rejection
cards.x:
Acute rejection is best pictured as a round trip. The graft brings its own dendritic cells with it. Those cells leave the graft and travel to the spleen, where they activate the recipient's effector T cells. The activated T cells then return through the blood to the graft and destroy it, in this example a transplanted kidney.

No antibody appears anywhere in this story, and that is what makes it type IV rather than the antibody-driven type II seen in hyperacute rejection. The trigger is a difference in human leukocyte antigens between donor and recipient.

cards.t: Why cornea, liver and bone marrow transplants behave differently
q: why do cornea transplants not need a tissue match
why is the liver tolerant
which transplant is most sensitive to HLA mismatch
cards.x:
Not every organ needs the same degree of matching.
- Cornea (the first organ successfully transplanted): it succeeds even without a human leukocyte antigen match. The eye downregulates T cells, macrophages, neutrophils and complement so that inflammation cannot impair vision.
- Liver: human leukocyte antigens are not assessed, but blood type (the A, B, O groups) is. Its architecture and vascularization help. Hepatocytes (liver cells) carry very little class I and no class II histocompatibility molecules (the self-markers other immune cells inspect). Constant exposure to digestive proteins also makes it tolerant.
- Bone marrow: the most sensitive to human leukocyte antigen discrepancies. Donors are matched on at least 10 markers, and even that does not always prevent graft versus host disease. Marrow is used for genetic disorders and cancers.

cards.t: Graft versus host disease
q: what is graft versus host disease
why does bone marrow transplant cause graft versus host disease
what organs does graft versus host disease affect
cards.x: Graft versus host disease is rejection in reverse: instead of the recipient attacking the graft, the donor's cells attack the recipient's tissue. It is a type IV (T cell) reaction. It is a particular danger with bone marrow transplants, since marrow is the tissue most sensitive to human leukocyte antigen discrepancies, and it affects about 30% of marrow recipients. It is systemic, with skin rash and involvement of muscle, liver and the gastrointestinal tract.

cards.t: Minimizing graft rejection: tissue matching and immunosuppression
q: how is transplant rejection prevented
what drugs suppress rejection
what is tissue typing
cards.x: Rejection is limited in two ways. First, match the tissue. Human leukocyte antigens are matched by tissue typing, including a mixed lymphocyte reaction, so that donor and recipient look as similar as possible to the immune system. Second, suppress the recipient's immune response with immunosuppressive drugs: purine analogs, corticosteroids, tacrolimus and cyclosporine, and rapamycin (sirolimus).

cards.t: Autoimmunity: when the immune system attacks self
q: what is autoimmunity
why do autoimmune diseases happen
which hypersensitivity types are involved in autoimmunity
cards.x:
Autoimmunity is what happens when the immune system loses tolerance to the body's own antigens (autoantigens). It then makes autoantibodies and sensitized T cells against them and destroys self tissue. Autoimmune disease can involve every hypersensitivity type except type I. The damage may come from antibody on cell surfaces (type II), immune complexes (type III) or T cells (type IV).

Two patterns are worth knowing. There are genetic and gender predispositions: autoimmune conditions run in families, and women are affected more often than men. And the disruption can be systemic, spread through the whole body, or organ specific, aimed at one tissue.

cards.t: Sequestered antigen theory (why eye trauma can hit both eyes)
q: what is the sequestered antigen theory
why would trauma to one eye affect the other eye
which tissues are immunologically privileged
cards.x:
The sequestered antigen theory explains autoimmunity by hidden tissue. Some tissues are immunologically privileged while the embryo grows, meaning the immune system effectively leaves them alone. The central nervous system, the lens of the eye, the thyroid and the testes are the examples. If one of them is damaged later in life, it releases antigens that the immune system sees as foreign, and it attacks.

The example is trauma to one eye. It releases intraocular antigens, which activate T cells, and those T cells attack both eyes, not just the injured one. Notice that no infection is involved, which makes this a noninfectious route to autoimmunity.

cards.t: Molecular mimicry
q: what is molecular mimicry
how does rheumatic fever cause autoimmunity
which infections trigger autoimmune disease through mimicry
cards.x:
Molecular mimicry is a case of the immune system doing its normal job and still causing autoimmunity. A microbe carries an antigen that looks similar to one of the body's own antigens, so the response against the microbe cross-reacts with self tissue.

The examples:
- Rheumatic fever: a cross-reactive streptococcal antigen makes antibodies that react with heart tissue.
- Lyme disease arthritis: triggered by infection with Borrelia burgdorferi.
- Reactive arthritis: triggered by infection with Shigella, Salmonella or Campylobacter.
- Type 1 diabetes: linked to coxsackie virus A and B, echovirus and rubella.

cards.t: Thymic senescence (the aging thymus)
q: what is thymic senescence
why does the thymus matter in autoimmunity
what happens to the thymus with age
cards.x:
Thymic senescence means the thymus ages. The thymus is the organ where T cells develop, and it is most active in fetal and early newborn life. After that it involutes, shrinking and being replaced by fat.

The link to disease is that premature thymic aging is a common feature in young people with autoimmune disorders. Decreased thymic output may mean T cells develop less efficiently, which could lead to more opportunistic infection, cancer and autoimmunity. How exactly this causes autoimmunity is unclear.

cards.t: Graves' disease vs Hashimoto's thyroiditis
q: what is the difference between Graves and Hashimoto
why does Graves disease cause hyperthyroidism
which autoimmune thyroid disease destroys follicle cells
cards.x:
Both diseases attack the thyroid follicle cells, which secrete thyroxine, but they push the thyroxine level in opposite directions.
- Graves' disease: autoantibodies attach to receptors on the thyroxine-secreting follicle cells. The cells make more thyroxine, so the result is hyperthyroidism.
- Hashimoto's thyroiditis: autoantibodies and T cells destroy the follicle cells. Less thyroxine is made, so the result is hypothyroidism.

A quick way to keep them straight: in Graves' the antibody stimulates the cell; in Hashimoto's the immune attack destroys it.

cards.t: Type 1 diabetes, myasthenia gravis and multiple sclerosis
q: what is the autoimmune basis of myasthenia gravis
what does the immune system attack in multiple sclerosis
how does type 1 diabetes relate to autoimmunity
cards.x:
Each of these autoimmune diseases has a target and a result.
- Type 1 diabetes: the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas are attacked, so insulin is reduced.
- Myasthenia gravis: autoantibodies bind acetylcholine receptors, which causes pronounced muscle weakness.
- Multiple sclerosis: T cells and autoantibodies damage the myelin sheath, the insulating coat around nerve fibers, producing a potentially paralyzing disease. It may follow Epstein-Barr virus or a retrovirus infection.

cards.t: Primary vs secondary immunodeficiency
q: what is the difference between primary and secondary immunodeficiency
what causes secondary immunodeficiency
which parts of the immune system can be deficient
cards.x:
Immunodeficiency means parts of the immune response are absent, and any of four components can be involved: B cells, T cells, phagocytes and complement. The two categories differ in when and why.
- Primary: present from birth (congenital), usually from genetic errors. Examples are agammaglobulinemia, DiGeorge syndrome, severe combined immunodeficiency, and complement and phagocyte deficiencies.
- Secondary: acquired after birth, from natural or artificial agents. Causes include infection and organic disease, such as the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which targets T helper cells and suppresses immunity overall. Chemotherapy or radiation and cancers of the blood cells also cause it.

Short version: primary is born with it; secondary is something that happens to you.

cards.t: Agammaglobulinemia, DiGeorge syndrome and severe combined immunodeficiency
q: why does DiGeorge syndrome cause fungal and viral infections
what is severe combined immunodeficiency
what infections come with a B cell deficiency
cards.x:
A good way to picture the primary immunodeficiencies is a developmental map in which a block at one spot predicts which infections follow.
- Block on the B cell limb: agammaglobulinemia. No antibodies are made, so the result is more bacterial infections.
- Block on the T cell limb: DiGeorge syndrome, where the thymus is missing or abnormal. The result is fungal, protozoan, helminth and viral infections.
- Block at the stem cell, where both limbs fail: severe combined immunodeficiency. Both lymphocyte limbs are missing or defective, so there is no adaptive response at all.

Adenosine deaminase deficiency is one cause of some types of severe combined immunodeficiency, a congenital, primary defect.

cards.t: How cancer arises: transformation, oncogenes, benign vs malignant
q: how does cancer develop
what is the difference between a benign and a malignant tumor
which viruses cause cancer
cards.x:
Cancer cells carry genetic changes that disrupt the normal cell division cycle. Possible causes are errors in mitosis (cell division), genetic damage, activation of oncogenes, or retroviruses. A cancer arises from a single cell that has piled up multiple mutations, and oncogenes can be switched on by radiation, chemicals or oncogenic viruses. Examples of the viruses are papillomavirus (cervical carcinoma) and hepatitis B virus (liver cancer).

Tumors can be benign, meaning nonspreading and self-contained, or malignant, meaning they spread from the tissue of origin to other sites. Meanwhile immune surveillance keeps cancer in check, which is why immune failure matters.

cards.t: What cancer cells do differently
q: what are the characteristics of cancer cells
what is angiogenesis
what does metastasis mean
cards.x:
Cancer cells share a set of behaviors that let them keep growing.
- They stimulate their own growth and ignore signals that inhibit growth.
- They avoid death by apoptosis (programmed cell death).
- They develop a blood supply of their own, called angiogenesis.
- They leave their site of origin to invade other tissues, called metastasis.
- They replicate constantly, and they evade and outrun the immune response.

cards.t: Tumor specific vs tumor associated antigens
q: what is the difference between tumor specific and tumor associated antigens
where do tumor antigens come from
cards.x:
Tumor antigens are markers on tumor cells that the immune system can recognize, and the two kinds differ by where they appear.
- Tumor specific antigens are found on tumor cells but not on normal cells. They are derived from viral proteins, mutated cellular proteins or amino acid recombinations.
- Tumor associated antigens are found on tumor cells and also on normal cells, only in smaller amounts.

So a tumor specific antigen is a cleaner target, because normal cells do not carry it.

cards.t: How tumors escape natural killer cells
q: how do tumors evade natural killer cells
what does cleaving the stress molecule do for a tumor
cards.x: Natural killer cells and gamma-delta T cells find tumor cells by recognizing a stress molecule displayed on the tumor cell's surface. A variant tumor cell gets around this by cleaving that stress molecule off its surface. The cut-off molecule floats away in soluble form and binds the killing receptor on the natural killer cell or gamma-delta T cell. With its receptor occupied by the decoy, the killer cell fails to attack, and the tumor cell escapes being killed.

cards.t: How tumors suppress immunity (TGF-beta and regulatory T cells)
q: how do tumors suppress the immune response
what do regulatory T cells do in a tumor
why do more regulatory T cells mean a worse prognosis
cards.x:
Successful tumors do more than hide. They actively turn immunity down. They secrete transforming growth factor beta, which suppresses immunity and recruits regulatory T cells. Those regulatory T cells make even more of it, plus interleukin 10. Together these suppress the cytotoxic T cells and type 1 helper T cells that are specific for tumor antigens, the very cells that should be attacking the tumor.

The practical consequence is that in many cancers, the more regulatory T cells there are in a tumor, the worse the prognosis.

cards.t: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
q: how do immune checkpoint inhibitors work
do checkpoint inhibitors kill cancer cells directly
which cancers are treated with checkpoint inhibitors
cards.x: Checkpoint proteins act as an off switch on T cells. When a checkpoint protein binds its partner, the T cell gets an off signal and stops. Checkpoint inhibitors block that binding, so the off signal never arrives and the T cells keep killing. Notice they do not kill cancer cells directly; they release the brake on the T cells that do. They are used for melanoma and some lung cancers.

cards.t: Adoptive cell therapy (tumor infiltrating lymphocytes and CAR-T)
q: what is adoptive cell therapy
what is CAR-T therapy used for
which adoptive cell therapies are approved
cards.x:
In adoptive cell therapy, the patient's own cells are engineered outside the body and then returned. There are three versions, at different stages.
- Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes: cytotoxic T cells expanded to a therapeutic amount. Approved for advanced melanoma (lifileucel, 2024) and still being studied in other solid tumors.
- Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells: approved for blood cancers.
- Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer cells: mostly in trials, including for solid tumors.

cards.t: Monoclonal antibodies in cancer
q: how are monoclonal antibodies used against cancer
what does anti-CD30 with auristatin do
how does a radionuclide antibody work
cards.x:
Monoclonal antibodies are used both to diagnose cancer and to eliminate cancer cells. More than 100 are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. The clever part is that an antibody can act as a delivery truck, carrying a chemotherapy drug or a radionuclide straight to the cancer cell.

Two examples:
- An antibody against CD20 (a target on B cells) carries a radionuclide. It irradiates malignant B cells.
- An antibody against CD30 (a target on lymphoma cells) carries auristatin. It stops lymphoma cells from forming a mitotic spindle, the structure they need to divide.

cards.t: Cytokine therapy: interleukin 2, interferon alpha and growth factors
q: how is interleukin 2 used against cancer
what does interferon alpha do in cancer treatment
which growth factors are used in cancer care
cards.x:
Cytokine therapy gives the signaling molecules that boost immune cells.
- Interleukin 2 (aldesleukin): increases cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells. Used for metastatic kidney cancer and melanoma.
- Interferon alpha: activates natural killer cells and dendritic cells. Used for melanoma, Kaposi's sarcoma and several blood cancers.
- Growth factors: erythropoietin supports red cells and interleukin 11 supports platelets.

cards.t: Coley's toxins
q: what were Coley's toxins
who first used infection to treat cancer
cards.x: Coley's toxins are an early historical example of cancer immunotherapy. In the 1890s, bone sarcomas were seen to regress when patients had a streptococcal skin infection. The treatment that followed was a mix of killed streptococci and Serratia marcescens. It fell from favor when radiation and chemotherapy arrived.

cards.t: Oncolytic viruses
q: how do oncolytic viruses work
what is the challenge with oncolytic virus therapy
is any oncolytic virus approved in the United States
cards.x: Oncolytic viruses are viruses used as cancer treatment. They infect both normal and cancer cells, but they replicate in and lyse (burst) only the tumor cells. Some occur naturally, such as mumps, and others are engineered. The main challenge is that the immune system may clear the virus before it can do its work. A few are approved, and just one in the United States, for melanoma.

cards.t: Cancer vaccines (prophylactic vs therapeutic)
q: what is the difference between a prophylactic and therapeutic cancer vaccine
how does BCG treat bladder cancer
which vaccines prevent cancer
cards.x:
Cancer vaccines come in two kinds.
- Prophylactic vaccines prevent a cancer-causing infection. Hepatitis B vaccine prevents the infection that leads to liver cancer (hepatocarcinoma), and papillomavirus vaccine prevents the infection that leads to reproductive cancers.
- Therapeutic vaccines activate immunity against tumor antigens in someone who already has the cancer. Examples are Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, a weakened tuberculosis microbe, for bladder cancer, and sipuleucel-T for metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer.

So the first kind stops the virus; the second trains the immune system against the tumor.

cards.t: Cancer immunotherapy strategies compared
q: what are the strategies of cancer immunotherapy
how do the immunotherapy strategies differ
which immunotherapy releases the brake on T cells
cards.x:
Cancer immunotherapy means getting the immune system to do the work, and the strategies differ by what they hand to the immune system.
- Release a brake: immune checkpoint inhibitors block the off signal so T cells keep killing.
- Give new or boosted cells: adoptive cell therapy returns the patient's own engineered cells.
- Give a targeted missile: monoclonal antibodies find cancer cells and can carry a chemotherapy drug or radionuclide.
- Give signals: cytokines such as interleukin 2 and interferon alpha boost immune cells.
- Use infection: Coley's toxins (historical) and oncolytic viruses, which lyse only tumor cells.
- Train the immune system: cancer vaccines, either preventing a cancer-causing infection or activating immunity against tumor antigens.

Each of these has its own card with the details.

cards.t: Three ways to identify a microbe: phenotypic, genotypic, immunological
q: what are the three categories of microbial identification
which identification methods need culture
what does phenotypic mean
cards.x:
Microbes can be identified by what they look like and do, by their genes, or by how the immune system reacts to them.
- Phenotypic: the observable microscopic and macroscopic features (phenotype means the physical expression of genes). These are shape, physiology and biochemistry, chemical analysis, and sensitivity to antimicrobial drugs. They usually need the microbe grown in culture, so they may take longer.
- Genotypic: the genetic makeup. Methods are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequence analysis, restriction fragment length polymorphism, gene sequencing and electrophoresis. These usually do not need culture.
- Immunological: serology, meaning antibody-antigen reactions. Examples are agglutination, precipitation, complement fixation, immunofluorescence and immunoassays. Culture may or may not be needed, but they always rely on antigen-antibody specificity.

A specimen can also go down two routes. Direct testing looks at the specimen itself and is fast. Culture and isolation grows the microbe first. It is slower but allows more tests.

cards.t: Rapid immunological tests and why you need a hypothesis first
q: why do you need a hypothesis before ordering a rapid test
how fast is the rapid strep test
what is the difference between presumptive and confirmatory results
cards.x:
Immune tests are generally easier and faster than hunting for the microbe itself, though a negative rapid test can still miss infection. The rapid strep test, for example, takes 10 to 15 minutes. The catch is that you have to know what to look for: each rapid test answers one question, so you need a hypothesis to pick the right one. Fever, a sore throat and pus pockets on the tonsils suggest strep throat, and only then does the rapid test give a useful answer.

Results also come in two categories, presumptive (probably this microbe) or confirmatory (definitely it).

cards.t: Genotypic methods: probes, restriction fragments and sequencing
q: what is the advantage of genotypic methods
what is 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing used for
how does restriction fragment length polymorphism work
cards.x:
Genotypic methods read the microbe's genetic makeup, and their big advantage is that no culture is needed. That matters most for slow-growing microbes such as Mycobacterium and hard-to-grow ones such as Legionella, because the long wait for culture is skipped. Precise, automated methods also give quick results, and a faster, more accurate diagnosis means the right treatment starts sooner.
- DNA probe hybridization: probes complementary to a microbe's specific sequences bind to it.
- Restriction fragment length polymorphism (DNA fingerprinting): restriction enzymes cut DNA into fragments whose lengths differ between microbes.
- Ribosomal RNA sequencing: compares base sequences to establish relationships and build phylogenetic (family) trees, using 16S ribosomal RNA genes for bacteria and 18S for eukaryotes.

cards.t: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
q: what does PCR do
what is a thermal cycler
does guanine plus cytosine content identify a species
cards.x:
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a way to make many copies of a specific piece of DNA or RNA. A machine called a thermal cycler amplifies the chosen piece. Making many copies like this is called amplification. The basic concept was invented by Kary Mullis and colleagues.

A related measure is the guanine plus cytosine content of the genetic material. It helps with taxonomic determination (placing a microbe in the family tree) but does not necessarily identify a specific microbe.

cards.t: Serology, titer and serotyping
q: what is serology
what does a titer measure
what is the difference between serological diagnosis and serotyping
cards.x:
Serology is diagnostic testing of serum (the liquid part of blood) in the lab. Antibodies are extremely specific for their antigens, so these methods can tell close relatives apart, and they are also very sensitive, able to detect small amounts. The result shows up as a precipitate, a color change or released radioactivity. The test tells you not only whether an antibody is present but how much, called the titer, often reported in binding antibody units.

There are two directions. In serological diagnosis, a known antigen is used to test a patient's serum for antibody. In serotyping, a known antibody is used to identify an unknown microbe.

cards.t: Agglutination vs precipitation tests
q: what is the difference between agglutination and precipitation
what is agglutination used for
what is the Weil-Felix test
cards.x:
Both are antibody-antigen reactions you can see, and the difference is the antigen.
- Agglutination: the antigen is whole-cell or insoluble. Antibody cross-links it into large visible clumps that sink to the bottom, so it can be read without instruments and run on a card or glass plate. It is generally more sensitive than precipitation. Uses: blood typing, rapid syphilis diagnosis, cold agglutinins for mycoplasmas, the Weil-Felix test for rickettsial disease and latex agglutination pregnancy tests. Color-changing rapid strep tests are a modified agglutination technique.
- Precipitation: the antigen is soluble, and antibody makes it insoluble, forming a visible precipitate in a gel or liquid. It is very sensitive. Uses: tube precipitation, Ouchterlony double diffusion in agar gel, and immunoelectrophoresis, which identifies which antibody class (immunoglobulin G, M and so on) binds antigen in serum.

cards.t: Southern, Northern, Western and Eastern blots
q: what does each blot detect
which blot is used to confirm HIV
what is the difference between Southern and Northern blots
cards.x:
The blots are a family of tests that separate molecules by electrophoresis and then detect a specific one. Each blot is for a different kind of molecule. The original, the Southern blot (invented by Edwin Southern around 1975), detects specific DNA sequences. The others were named by playing on his name, using the other compass points.
- Northern (about 1977): RNA, to study gene expression. Useful for oncogenes and transplant rejection.
- Western (about 1981): proteins, by electrophoresis and then an immunoassay, with bands where antibody binds. It was long used as the second test to confirm human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) status. Current United States guidance has replaced it with a second immunoassay and nucleic acid testing. It is also used in testing for bovine spongiform encephalopathy and Lyme disease.
- Eastern (about 1982): proteins, lipids and carbohydrate epitopes, such as post-translational products.

cards.t: The complement fixation test (why lysis means negative)
q: how does the complement fixation test work
what does hemolysis mean in a complement fixation test
why is complement fixation counter-intuitive
cards.x:
The complement fixation test is counter-intuitive, because lysis (the red cells bursting) is the negative result. It uses four components: antigen, antibody (lysin), complement and sensitized sheep red blood cells.

The logic runs like this. If the patient's serum contains the antibody, it meets the antigen and uses up (fixes) the complement. No complement is left to burst the sheep red cells, so there is no hemolysis, the tube stays red, and the test is positive. If there is no antibody, the complement stays free, bursts the sheep cells, and the tube turns clear: negative. The test has now been largely replaced by the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.

cards.t: Direct vs indirect fluorescent antibody tests
q: what is the difference between direct and indirect fluorescent antibody testing
which fluorescent test detects the patient's antibody
cards.x:
In fluorescent antibody testing, a monoclonal antibody labeled with a fluorescent dye makes cells or clumps glow under the microscope. The whole distinction is what you are looking for.
- Direct: the fluorescent antibody binds the unknown microbe or tissue itself, so it identifies the antigen.
- Indirect: the patient's serum is laid on a known antigen, and a second, fluorescent anti-antibody shows whether the serum's antibody stuck. So it detects the patient's antibody.

In the indirect version, no antibody in the serum means nothing for the second antibody to bind, and no glow.

cards.t: Immunoassays: radioimmunoassay and ELISA
q: how does an ELISA work
what is the difference between indirect and capture ELISA
what is a radioimmunoassay
cards.x:
Immunoassays are extremely sensitive tests that detect trace amounts of antigen or antibody. A radioimmunoassay uses labels of radioactive isotopes. The enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) uses an enzyme attached to an antibody; when its substrate is added, the enzyme makes a colored product (a chromogen). It is run in 96-well plates, and color appears only where the enzyme-linked antibody stayed bound.

There are two designs. In the indirect assay the well is coated with known antigen to catch a patient's antibody, which is the basis of human immunodeficiency virus screening. In the capture (sandwich) assay the well is coated with antibody to catch an antigen between two antibodies, as used for measles virus.

cards.t: In vivo tests and why viruses are hard to diagnose
q: what is an in vivo test
why are viruses difficult to culture
what is an example of in vivo diagnostic testing
cards.x:
In vivo testing differs from serology in where the reaction happens: antigen is introduced directly into the body to find out whether antibody or sensitivity is present. The tuberculin skin test and allergy testing are the named examples.

Viruses cause a special difficulty. They are not cells and need a specific host cell to replicate, so culturing them is labor intensive. Some rapid point-of-care tests use antigen-antibody reactions.

cards.t: Phenotypic identification: morphology, biochemical tests and chemical analysis
q: what does phenotypic identification look at
what is macroscopic morphology
what are the common biochemical tests
cards.x:
Phenotypic identification reads the microbe's physiology and metabolism. The four things looked at:
- Microscopic morphology: fresh or stained microbes. You look at cell shape, size, stain reaction (Gram, flagellar, acid-fast) and cell structures. The Gram and acid-fast stains, with direct fluorescent antibody and direct antigen testing, give immediate direct examination. It reports before anything is cultured.
- Macroscopic morphology: colony appearance on test plates, seen with the naked eye. You note texture, size, shape, pigment and growth requirements.
- Physiological or biochemical: whether particular enzymes or metabolic pathways are present. If a product forms, the enzyme is present. Common tests are carbohydrate fermentation, amino acid utilization, hydrolysis of gelatin, starch or lipids, catalase, oxidase, coagulase and hemolysins.
- Chemical analysis: specific chemical composition, such as cell wall peptides and cell membrane lipids.

cards.t: Blood agar, chocolate agar and mannitol salts agar
q: what is blood agar used for
is chocolate agar anaerobic
what does mannitol salts agar select for
cards.x:
These three plates each answer a different question.
- Blood agar detects hemolytic activity, whether the microbe bursts red blood cells.
- Chocolate agar is an enriched medium for fastidious (picky) microbes. They are grown in extra carbon dioxide, for example in a candle jar, not anaerobically.
- Mannitol salts agar selects for salt tolerance, because only microbes that withstand the high salt grow, and differentiates by the pH change when mannitol is fermented.

cards.t: Simmons citrate, triple sugar iron, urea broth and API strips
q: what does a blue Simmons citrate result mean
what does hot pink urea broth mean
what is an API 20E strip
cards.x:
These tests read a color change that reports on the microbe's metabolism.
- Simmons citrate tests citrate utilization. Using citrate raises the pH, and the indicator bromthymol blue turns blue.
- Triple sugar iron slant shows several pH changes on a single slant.
- Urea broth tests urea hydrolysis. Breaking down urea raises the pH, and hot pink means urease is present.
- Rapid test strips (API 20E) put many biochemical tests on one strip.

Two other approaches: bacteriophage typing checks susceptibility to phages, and animal inoculation grows a microbe in an animal, for example Mycobacterium leprae.

cards.t: Is the microbe causing the disease? Normal flora and Koch's postulates
q: how do you know if a recovered microbe causes the disease
what are Koch's postulates for
which virulence enzymes are used as tests
cards.x:
Finding a microbe in a patient does not prove it caused the illness, because it might just be normal flora. So the diagnostic question is whether the microbe recovered is actually causing the disease. That is the reasoning behind Koch's postulates, in their traditional and molecular forms.

Some virulence enzymes are themselves the test: hemolysins on blood agar and coagulase are among the common tests.

cards.t: Specimen collection, handling and safety
q: how should specimens be handled
do universal precautions eliminate infection risk
what affects diagnostic results from a specimen
cards.x:
Every specimen should be considered potentially infectious. The result you get depends on how the specimen was collected, handled, transported and stored. Some need a preservative or fixative. Others need cooling, heating or other special treatment. Collection sites and methods include the nasopharynx, throat, sputum, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, urine (by clean catch or catheter), feces, skin and genital swabs. A specimen then goes either to direct testing or to cultivation, isolation and identification.

Aseptic procedures and universal precautions (gloves, face shields, masks) reduce the risk of transmission but do not eliminate it.

cards.t: Antimicrobial sensitivity testing (Kirby-Bauer, concentration strips)
q: how does the Kirby-Bauer test work
what does a larger zone of inhibition mean
what is a minimum inhibitory concentration
cards.x:
Sensitivity testing answers which drug works against this microbe. In the Kirby-Bauer disk-diffusion test, disks of different drugs are placed on a plate of the microbe. The clear zone of inhibition around each disk shows where growth was stopped. For a given drug, a larger zone means the microbe is more susceptible to it. Zones of different drugs cannot be ranked against each other. The test shows which drugs the microbe is susceptible or resistant to.

Minimum inhibitory concentration strips give the same kind of answer as a number: the lowest concentration of drug that stops growth. As for treatment strategy, the key point is speed. Faster, more accurate (genotypic) diagnosis means proper treatment can begin in a timely manner.

cards.t: Telling staphylococci from streptococci (Gram stain, catalase, coagulase, salt)
q: how do you tell staphylococci from streptococci
what does the catalase test tell you
what does a positive coagulase test mean
cards.x:
Staphylococci and streptococci are both Gram-positive cocci. Gram-positive means a thick peptidoglycan layer in the cell envelope, which makes the cells physically strong (Gram-negative cells are chemically strong instead). Neither forms spores or moves, and both can make capsules and slime layers. They separate on a few quick tests.
- Arrangement: staphylococci sit in irregular clusters; streptococci form long chains, commonly seen in pairs.
- Catalase (add hydrogen peroxide): staphylococci are positive and bubble; streptococci are negative, although they have a peroxidase system. Enterococci are catalase negative too.
- Coagulase: this splits the staphylococci. Positive means Staphylococcus aureus; negative means one of the other staphylococci.
- Salt: staphylococci withstand high salt and grow on mannitol salts agar; streptococci do not grow well on it.

cards.t: Sorting streptococci: hemolysis, bacitracin and optochin
q: how do you identify a streptococcus on blood agar
what is the difference between alpha and beta hemolysis
what does optochin sensitivity identify
cards.x:
Streptococci are sorted first by what they do to red blood cells on a blood agar plate, then by one drug disk.
- Beta-hemolytic means complete hemolysis, a clear zone around the colony. If it is sensitive to bacitracin, it is group A, Streptococcus pyogenes. If it is resistant, it is group B or C.
- Alpha-hemolytic means partial hemolysis, a greenish zone. If it is sensitive to optochin, it is Streptococcus pneumoniae. If it is resistant, it is group D or a viridans streptococcus.

The word viridans comes from the green color of partial hemolysis.

cards.t: Staphylococcus aureus: features, carriage and who is at risk
q: what is Staphylococcus aureus
how common is Staphylococcus aureus carriage
who is predisposed to Staphylococcus aureus infection
cards.x:
Staphylococci are common residents of the skin and mucous membranes, and Staphylococcus aureus is the key species. On a plate it makes large, round, opaque colonies that may look slightly yellowish (aureus means golden). It grows best at 37 degrees Celsius and is a facultative anaerobe, so it thrives with or without oxygen. It also withstands high salt, extremes of pH and high temperatures, and it makes many virulence factors.

It is found in most places people frequent and is easily isolated from fomites (objects that carry germs). Carriage is 20 to 60% of healthy adults, mostly in the anterior nares (front of the nose), skin, nasopharynx and intestines. Infection is more likely with poor hygiene or nutrition, tissue injury, a preexisting primary infection, diabetes or immunodeficiency.

cards.t: Staphylococcus aureus enzymes: coagulase, hyaluronidase, penicillinase and more
q: what does coagulase do
what enzymes does Staphylococcus aureus make
why is Staphylococcus aureus resistant to penicillin
cards.x:
Staphylococcus aureus carries a toolkit of enzymes, and the names tell you the job.
- Coagulase coagulates plasma and blood. It is made by 97% of human isolates and is a significant diagnostic trait. That is why the coagulase test picks out Staphylococcus aureus from the other staphylococci.
- Hyaluronidase digests connective tissue, staphylokinase digests blood clots and deoxyribonuclease digests DNA.
- Lipases digest oils and other lipids, which enhances colonization of the skin.
- Penicillinase inactivates penicillin, which is why most staphylococci resist it. Beta-lactamase behaves similarly.

cards.t: Staphylococcus aureus toxins: hemolysins, leukocidin, enterotoxin and more
q: what toxins does Staphylococcus aureus produce
what does leukocidin do
which toxin causes scalded skin syndrome
cards.x:
Staphylococcus aureus makes several toxins, and three of them are each linked to a named disease: food intoxication, scalded skin syndrome and toxic shock syndrome.
- Hemolysins (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) lyse red blood cells, which is visible on blood agar.
- Leukocidin lyses leukocytes, especially neutrophils and macrophages.
- Enterotoxin induces gastrointestinal distress (food intoxication).
- Exfoliative toxin splits the upper layers of the epidermis apart (scalded skin syndrome).
- Toxic shock syndrome toxin induces fever, vomiting, shock and systemic organ damage.

cards.t: Staphylococcal skin infections: folliculitis, furuncle, carbuncle, impetigo
q: what is the difference between a furuncle and a carbuncle
what is folliculitis
who gets impetigo
cards.x:
These four are staphylococcal skin infections, and the first three involve hair follicles.
- Folliculitis: superficial inflammation of a hair follicle. It usually resolves but can progress.
- Furuncle (boil): inflammation of a hair follicle or sebaceous gland that progresses into an abscess or pustule, with bacteria and phagocytes walled off into a core of pus.
- Carbuncle: a larger, deeper lesion formed when a cluster of furuncles aggregates and interconnects.
- Impetigo: bubble-like swellings that break and peel away; most common in newborns.

The easy way to tell furuncle from carbuncle: one follicle versus several joined together.

cards.t: Osteomyelitis, bacteremia, food intoxication, scalded skin and toxic shock
q: why is staph food poisoning called an intoxication
what causes scalded skin syndrome
what causes toxic shock syndrome
cards.x:
Beyond the skin, Staphylococcus aureus causes several deeper and toxin-driven diseases.
- Osteomyelitis: infection is established in the metaphysis and an abscess forms.
- Bacteremia: bacteria in the blood. The primary origin is another infected site or a medical device, and endocarditis is a possible complication.
- Food intoxication: you swallow heat-stable enterotoxins that are already made, which causes gastrointestinal distress.
- Scalded skin syndrome: the toxin induces a bright red flush, then blisters, then desquamation (shedding) of the epidermis.
- Toxic shock syndrome: toxemia leading to shock and organ failure (see its own card for what does and does not cause it).

cards.t: Treating and preventing Staphylococcus aureus; MRSA
q: why is Staphylococcus aureus hard to treat
what is MRSA
how are staph abscesses treated
cards.x:
Treatment is difficult because 95% of staphylococci produce penicillinase, so they are resistant to penicillin and ampicillin. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) carries multiple resistance. Older teaching describes some strains as resisting everything except vancomycin. But vancomycin and several newer drugs still work against most strains. Methicillin resistance is increasingly community acquired, not just hospital acquired, so strains are labeled community-acquired or hospital-acquired. Abscesses have to be surgically perforated, with wounds kept thoroughly clean and covered. Systemic infections may need intensive, lengthy antimicrobial therapy.

For prevention, healthcare providers use universal precautions to prevent or at least reduce nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections. Everyone should keep up personal hygiene and avoid sharing towels, washcloths, razors or toothbrushes. In the lab, the bacteria can be isolated from pus, tissue exudates, sputum, urine and blood. They are identified by cultivation, the catalase reaction, biochemical testing and the coagulase reaction.

cards.t: Toxic shock syndrome (staphylococcal)
q: what causes toxic shock syndrome
is toxic shock syndrome sexually transmitted
is toxic shock always related to menstruation
cards.x:
Toxic shock syndrome is an illness driven by a toxin from Staphylococcus aureus, rather than by the bacteria themselves spreading through the body. The toxin induces fever, vomiting, shock and damage to several organs. It comes from Staphylococcus aureus that the person is already colonized or infected with, so it is not sexually transmitted. The classic association is improper tampon use in females, but about half of cases today are not related to menstruation.

A similar picture can also come from group A Streptococcus: streptococcal toxic shock syndrome is one of the systemic infections it causes.

cards.t: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (epidermidis, hominis, capitis, saprophyticus)
q: what diseases does Staphylococcus epidermidis cause
which coagulase-negative staph causes urinary tract infections
where does each coagulase-negative staphylococcus live
cards.x:
The coagulase-negative staphylococci are the staph species that fail the coagulase test. They are frequently implicated in nosocomial and opportunistic infections. They often start polymicrobial biofilms (communities of several microbes), which can lead to further complications.
- Staphylococcus epidermidis: lives on skin and mucous membranes. Causes endocarditis, bacteremia, urinary tract infection and wound infection.
- Staphylococcus hominis: lives around the apocrine sweat glands of the armpits and groin. Causes wound infection.
- Staphylococcus capitis: scalp, face and external ear. Causes wound infection.
- Staphylococcus saprophyticus: infrequently found on skin, intestine and vagina. May cause urinary tract infection.

The first three can all cause wound infections by penetrating broken skin.

cards.t: How streptococci are classified: Lancefield groups and hemolysis
q: what are Lancefield groups
which streptococci are beta-hemolytic
which streptococci are alpha-hemolytic
cards.x:
Streptococci are Gram-positive cocci in long chains, commonly in pairs. They do not form spores or move, can make capsules and slime layers, and are facultative anaerobes. They do not produce catalase but do have a peroxidase system. Most parasitic forms are fastidious (picky), needing enriched media, and grow as small, nonpigmented colonies on blood agar. They are very sensitive to drying, heat and disinfectants.

Two systems classify them. Lancefield grouping (Rebecca Lancefield, 1933) uses cell wall antigens called C-carbohydrates, giving groups A, B, C and so on. Hemolysis sorts them on blood agar: beta (complete) covers groups A, B, C, G and some D, while alpha (partial) covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and the viridans streptococci, named for the greenish color of partial hemolysis.

cards.t: The streptococci that cause human disease and what each one does
q: which streptococci are significant human pathogens
where does Streptococcus agalactiae live
what does Streptococcus mutans cause
cards.x:
The significant human streptococcal pathogens, with the usual place they live and what they cause:
- Streptococcus pyogenes: group A, beta-hemolytic. Human throat. Throat and skin infections and scarlet fever.
- Streptococcus agalactiae: group B, beta-hemolytic. Human vagina and cow udder. Neonatal and wound infections.
- Enterococcus faecalis: group D. Human and animal intestine. Endocarditis and urinary tract infection.
- Streptococcus sanguis and Streptococcus mutans: viridans, in the human oral cavity. Endocarditis and dental caries.
- Streptococcus pneumoniae: alpha-hemolytic. Human respiratory tract. Bacterial pneumonia.

Enterococcus was split off from Streptococcus in 1984 by 16S ribosomal RNA gene analysis, and the taxonomy is still evolving.

cards.t: Streptococcus pyogenes virulence factors (M-protein, capsule, streptolysins)
q: what virulence factors does Streptococcus pyogenes have
what does M-protein do
what does streptokinase do
cards.x:
Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) is the most serious of the streptococcal pathogens, and its virulence factors fall into two jobs: dodging the defenses, and causing damage and spread.

Dodging defenses:
- C-carbohydrates protect it against lysozyme.
- M-protein contributes to its resistance to phagocytosis.
- The hyaluronic acid capsule looks like the body's own hyaluronic acid, so it provokes little immune response.
- C5a protease hinders the complement and neutrophil response.

Damage and spread: fimbriae (short protein fibers) for adherence; streptolysins O and S, hemolysins that injure cells and tissue; erythrogenic (pyrogenic) toxin, which induces fever and the typical red rash; superantigens, strong stimulants of monocytes and lymphocytes that cause the release of tumor necrosis factor; and streptokinase (digests fibrin clots), hyaluronidase (breaks down connective tissue) and deoxyribonuclease (hydrolyzes DNA).

cards.t: Streptococcus pyogenes infections: strep throat, scarlet fever, skin
q: what infections does Streptococcus pyogenes cause
what causes scarlet fever
who gets strep infections and how are they spread
cards.x:
Humans are the only reservoir of Streptococcus pyogenes, and inapparent carriers exist. It spreads by contact, droplets, food and fomites, and enters through the skin or pharynx. Children are the group mainly affected, for both skin and throat infections.
- Streptococcal pharyngitis: strep throat.
- Scarlet fever: caused by a strain carrying a prophage that codes for erythrogenic toxin. It can lead to sequelae (later complications).
- Impetigo (pyoderma): superficial lesions that break and form a highly contagious crust, often in epidemics among schoolchildren, and also with insect bites, poor hygiene and crowding.
- Erysipelas: enters through a break in the skin and spreads to the dermis and subcutaneous tissues; it can stay superficial or become systemic.
- Septicemia, pneumonia and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome are the other systemic infections.

cards.t: Rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis and penicillin treatment after strep
q: what are the complications of untreated strep throat
what does rheumatic fever cause
how are group A and B streptococci treated
cards.x:
Untreated streptococcal infections can lead to later complications, called sequelae.
- Rheumatic fever follows overt or subclinical (silent) pharyngitis in children. It causes carditis with extensive valve damage, arthritis, chorea (jerky involuntary movements) and fever.
- Acute glomerulonephritis causes nephritis (kidney inflammation), increased blood pressure and occasionally heart failure. It can become chronic and lead to kidney failure.

Groups A and B are commonly treated with penicillin unless it is contraindicated (resistance or allergy). Long-term penicillin prophylaxis may be prescribed for people with a history of rheumatic fever. Antibiotic-resistant strains are a big problem.

cards.t: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) and the newborn
k: group B strep screening in pregnancy
q: why are pregnant women screened for group B Streptococcus
how does a newborn get group B strep
what antibiotic is used for group B Streptococcus in labor
how are pregnant women screened for group B Streptococcus
cards.x:
Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) regularly lives in the human vagina, pharynx and large intestine. The danger is to newborns. The bacteria can be transferred to the infant during vaginal delivery and cause severe infection. It is the most prevalent cause of neonatal pneumonia, sepsis and meningitis.

Because of this, pregnant women are screened late in pregnancy and treated. Screening is by vaginal-rectal swab culture (or a nucleic acid test), not by antibody detection. Intrapartum prophylaxis (treatment given during labor) is intravenous penicillin, with ampicillin as the alternative and other drugs for people allergic to penicillin. Streptomycin is not used. In debilitated patients the same bacteria also cause wound and skin infections and endocarditis.

cards.t: Enterococci (group D): Enterococcus faecalis, faecium and durans
q: what are enterococci
what infections do enterococci cause
why are enterococcal infections hard to treat
cards.x: The group D enterococci (Enterococcus faecalis, faecium and durans) are normal colonists of the human large intestine. They become a problem when the host is weak: they cause opportunistic urinary, wound and skin infections, particularly in debilitated people. Treatment usually requires multiple antibiotic therapy. Like the streptococci, they are catalase negative, which separates them from the staphylococci.

cards.t: Identifying streptococci: rapid tests, bacitracin, CAMP and bile esculin
q: what is the CAMP test
how are streptococci identified in the lab
what does a positive CAMP test look like
cards.x:
Getting the identification right ensures proper treatment and helps prevent complications. Rapid diagnostic tests use monoclonal antibodies that react with the C-carbohydrates. The culture-based (phenotypic) methods are the bacitracin disc sensitivity test, the CAMP (Christie, Atkins and Munch-Petersen, 1944) test and bile esculin hydrolysis.

The CAMP test works because a protein called CAMP factor teams up (works synergistically) with beta-hemolytic Staphylococcus aureus. Where the two streaks meet on the blood agar plate, the hemolysis widens into a flame or arrowhead shape. The test is time consuming. But it has been effective in detecting Listeria monocytogenes, a Gram-positive rod, from food and clinical specimens.

cards.t: Viridans streptococci, dental caries and subacute endocarditis
q: what are viridans streptococci
how do viridans streptococci cause endocarditis
why does Streptococcus mutans cause cavities
cards.x:
The viridans streptococci (including Streptococcus mutans, oralis, salivarius, sanguis, milleri and mitis) are partially hemolytic, leaving a greenish color around their colonies. They are the most numerous residents of the gums, teeth and oral cavity. They also live in the nasopharynx, genital tract and skin.

They are not very invasive on their own, but dental or surgical procedures may let them in. Streptococcus mutans makes slime layers that stick to teeth, the basis of plaque and dental caries (cavities). Disease includes gingivitis, periodontitis, bacteremia, meningitis, abdominal infection and tooth abscesses. The most serious is subacute endocarditis. Blood-borne bacteria settle on the heart lining or valves and colonize them by forming biofilms. People with preexisting heart disease are at high risk. So prophylactic antibiotics are given before surgery or dental work for certain preexisting heart conditions (many dentists have stopped except in extreme circumstances).

cards.t: Streptococcus pneumoniae: capsule, pneumonia and otitis media
q: what does Streptococcus pneumoniae look like
why is the capsule important in pneumococcus
how does the pneumococcus cause pneumonia and ear infections
cards.x:
Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is seen as small, lancet-shaped cells (pointed ovals) in pairs and short chains. It lives in the nasopharynx, where 5 to 50% of people carry it as normal flora. Its major virulence factor is the capsule: all pathogenic strains form large capsules, and the specific soluble substance in the capsule varies among types.

Two diseases to know. Pneumococcal pneumonia happens when the bacteria are aspirated into the lungs, where they multiply and provoke an overwhelming inflammatory response. Otitis media (middle ear infection) happens when they reach the middle ear by the eustachian tube.

In the lab it needs blood or chocolate agar and is capnophilic (carbon dioxide loving), with growth improved by 5 to 10% carbon dioxide. It is an aerotolerant anaerobe that lacks catalase, so cultures may die in high laboratory oxygen.

cards.t: Pneumococcal infection: who is at risk, treatment and vaccines
q: who is at risk for pneumococcal infection
how is pneumococcus treated and prevented
why are pneumococcal infections usually endogenous
cards.x:
Pneumococcal infections are usually endogenous, meaning they come from the person's own flora in the nasopharynx. The risk is greatest in the immunocompromised, young children, the elderly, people with other lung disease or a viral infection, and people in close quarters. The bacterium is very delicate and does not survive long outside its habitat.

Treatment was traditionally penicillin G or V, but drug resistance is increasing. Two vaccines exist for high-risk individuals: a capsular antigen vaccine for older adults, which is effective for about 5 years, and a conjugate vaccine for children 2 to 23 months. Pneumococcal vaccines are not given every year, and current United States adult schedules use conjugate vaccines as well.

cards.t: Neisseria: what they look like, how they grow and how they attach
q: what are the features of Neisseria
what does immunoglobulin A protease do
how are Neisseria cultured
cards.x:
Neisseria belong to the family Neisseriaceae. They are Gram-negative cocci, so they have only a thin layer of peptidoglycan. The two primary frank (true) pathogens are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitidis. They are bean-shaped diplococci with no flagella or spores. Capsules are common, and pili (short protein fibers made of pilin) enhance attachment.

They are strict parasites that do not survive long outside the human host. They are aerobic or microaerophilic (needing a low oxygen concentration) and produce both catalase and cytochrome oxidase. In the lab, the pathogenic species need enriched complex media and carbon dioxide-enhanced chambers, such as chocolate agar in a candle jar.

For virulence they use fimbriae and other surface molecules to attach and slow phagocytosis. They also make immunoglobulin A protease, which cleaves secretory immunoglobulin A, the protective antibody of mucous membranes such as the genitourinary tract.

cards.t: Gonorrhea: spread, symptoms in men and women, and complications
q: what does Neisseria gonorrhoeae cause
why can gonorrhea cause infertility
how does a newborn get gonococcal conjunctivitis
cards.x:
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is strictly a human pathogen and one of the top 5 sexually transmitted diseases. It takes only 100 to 1,000 cells to infect, and it survives no more than 1 to 2 hours on fomites (objects an infected person has touched). Many infections are silent: about 10% of males and 50% of females have no symptoms.
- Males: urethritis with a yellowish discharge, and scarring that can lead to infertility.
- Females: vaginitis and urethritis, then salpingitis (pelvic inflammatory disease) as infection climbs from the cervix through the uterus into the fallopian tube. Tubal scarring explains the common sterility and ectopic tubal pregnancy.
- Extragenital: anal and pharyngeal infection, conjunctivitis, septicemia and arthritis.
- Newborns: gonococcal conjunctivitis from the birth canal, an eye inflammation that can cause blindness.

cards.t: Diagnosing, treating and controlling gonorrhea
q: how is gonorrhea diagnosed
how is gonorrhea treated now
why is newborn eye prophylaxis given
do women with gonorrhea need a cesarean section
cards.x:
The classic presumptive diagnosis is a Gram stain showing Gram-negative (pink) intracellular diplococci, meaning inside neutrophils, in urethral, vaginal, cervical or eye exudate (pus).

Control rests on several points.
- 20 to 30% of new cases are penicillinase-producing or tetracycline-resistant strains.
- No long-term immunity is acquired, so infections recur. It is a reportable disease.
- The newborn can pick it up in the birth canal, so topical antibiotic prophylaxis goes into the newborn's eyes immediately after birth.
- Current treatment guidance is a single cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), with doxycycline added only when chlamydia has not been excluded.
- In pregnancy, gonorrhea is treated with antibiotics, and a cesarean section is not routinely needed.

cards.t: Neisseria meningitidis: how it reaches the meninges, and who is at risk
q: how does Neisseria meningitidis cause meningitis
who is at high risk for meningococcal disease
why is meningococcal disease so dangerous
cards.x:
