Neisseria meningitidis (the meningococcus) is a prevalent cause of meningitis, sporadic or epidemic. Its reservoir is the nasopharynx of 3 to 30% of adults, higher in institutional settings. Risk is highest in close quarters (college dorms and apartments), in children 6 months to 3 years, and at ages 10 to 20. Current figures put the peaks in infants under 1 year and in adolescents and young adults (about 16 to 23).

Its virulence factors are a capsule, adhesive fimbriae, immunoglobulin A protease and endotoxin. The path to disease starts in the nasopharynx. The bacteria enter the bloodstream, cross the blood-brain barrier, permeate the meninges and grow in the cerebrospinal fluid. Onset is very rapid with neurological symptoms, and endotoxin causes hemorrhage and shock, so it can be fatal.

cards.t: Diagnosing, treating and preventing meningococcal disease
q: how is meningococcal meningitis diagnosed
who gets prophylaxis after a meningococcal case
what is in the meningococcal vaccine
cards.x:
Diagnosis starts with a Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid, blood or a nasopharyngeal sample. Culture is needed to tell the bacteria apart from look-alikes but is time consuming, so diagnosis may be delayed; rapid tests for the capsular polysaccharide exist.

Treatment is intravenous penicillin G or a cephalosporin. Prophylaxis is given to close contacts such as family and children nearby, and to medical personnel only after direct exposure to the patient's secretions. Vaccines exist too: the A, C, W and Y vaccines contain purified capsular antigens, while the serogroup B vaccines are built on surface proteins instead.

cards.t: Moraxella (Branhamella) catarrhalis and Acinetobacter baumannii
q: who gets Moraxella infections
what is Acinetobacter baumannii
where are Acinetobacter infections acquired
cards.x:
Moraxella and Acinetobacter are two bacteria that cause trouble mostly in vulnerable or hospitalized people. Branhamella catarrhalis, now classified as Moraxella, is a diplococcus on the mucous membranes of humans and other primates. It is found in the nasopharynx. It is a significant opportunist in cancer, diabetic and alcoholic patients. It is also a common cause of childhood otitis media (middle ear infection), one of the three classic bacterial causes. It was moved into the genus Moraxella by 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing.

Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant coccobacillus (a shape between a ball and a rod) and an important hospital-acquired infection, especially in military hospitals. The genus Acinetobacter is common in soil and water, but A. baumannii itself is rarely isolated from soil. Infections in service members wounded in Iraq and Afghanistan were traced to spread inside military hospitals, not to the soil.

cards.t: Reservoirs and transmission of the staphylococci and streptococci
q: how is Staphylococcus aureus spread
how is group B Streptococcus transmitted
where does each coccus live in the body
cards.x:
Where each coccus lives, and how it gets in:
- Staphylococcus aureus: anterior nares (20 to 60% of adults), skin, nasopharynx, intestines and fomites. It enters through wounds, follicles or glands, spreads from another infected site or a medical device (bacteremia), and causes food intoxication through heat-stable enterotoxin. Toxic shock is classically linked to improper tampon use (it is a toxin illness, not sexually transmitted). Resistant strains spread in the community as well as hospitals, and shared towels, razors and toothbrushes pass it on.
- Coagulase-negative staphylococci: skin, mucous membranes and apocrine glands. They enter by penetrating broken skin and are nosocomial and opportunistic.
- Streptococcus pyogenes: humans only, in the throat, nasopharynx and occasionally skin; inapparent carriers. It spreads by contact, droplets, food and fomites, mostly in children.
- Group B Streptococcus: vagina, pharynx, large intestine. Transferred to the infant during vaginal delivery.
- Enterococci live in the large intestine and cause opportunistic infections. Viridans streptococci live in the gums and teeth and enter through dental or surgical procedures. The pneumococcus lives in the nasopharynx (5 to 50%) and is endogenous, reaching the lungs by aspiration or the middle ear by the eustachian tube.

cards.t: Reservoirs and transmission of Neisseria, Moraxella and Acinetobacter
q: how is Neisseria gonorrhoeae transmitted
how does Neisseria meningitidis spread
how is Acinetobacter baumannii acquired
cards.x:
The Gram-negative cocci each have a clear home and route.
- Neisseria gonorrhoeae: strictly human. Spread by sexual contact (low infectious dose; survives 1 to 2 hours on fomites, meaning objects), and to newborns through the birth canal.
- Neisseria meningitidis: lives in the nasopharynx (3 to 30% of adults). Spreads in close quarters such as dormitories, and moves from the nasopharynx into the bloodstream and across the blood-brain barrier.
- Moraxella: lives in the nasopharynx and is an opportunist in cancer, diabetic and alcoholic patients.
- Acinetobacter baumannii: hospital environments. It is hospital acquired, especially in military hospitals, rather than coming from soil.

cards.t: What a candle jar and chocolate agar actually do
q: is chocolate agar used for anaerobes
what does a candle jar do
how are Neisseria grown in the lab
cards.x: A candle jar raises the carbon dioxide level to a few percent but leaves most of the oxygen, so it is not an anaerobic setup. Chocolate agar is an enriched medium for fastidious (picky) microbes such as Neisseria and the pneumococcus, often incubated in extra carbon dioxide. Neisseria are aerobic or microaerophilic, not anaerobes.

cards.t: Meningococcal serogroups, age peaks and vaccine types
q: which serogroups cause meningococcal disease
why is the group B meningococcal vaccine different
who is at highest risk for meningococcal disease by age
cards.x:
Serogroups A, B, C, W, X and Y cause nearly all meningococcal disease. Current figures put the peaks in infants under 1 year and in adolescents and young adults (about ages 16 to 23).

The vaccines differ. The quadrivalent (A, C, W, Y) vaccines contain purified capsular antigens. The serogroup B vaccines are built on surface proteins instead, because the group B capsule is poorly immunogenic (it provokes little immune response).

cards.t: How the Gram-positive bacilli are sorted (spores, shape, acid-fast)
q: how are the Gram-positive bacilli classified
which Gram-positive rods form spores
what are the irregular Gram-positive rods
cards.x:
The medically important Gram-positive bacilli (rods) fall into three groups. They are sorted by two properties: whether they make endospores (tough dormant forms) and whether they are acid-fast. The groups are the endospore-formers, the non-endospore-formers and those of irregular shape and staining. Think of it as a series of questions.
- Spores? If yes, ask about oxygen. Bacillus is aerobic or facultative, and Clostridium is obligately anaerobic. The spore-forming genera are Bacillus, Clostridium, Clostridioides and Sporolactobacillus (not pathogenic).
- If no spores, is the shape regular? Regular rods stain uniformly and are not pleomorphic (shape-changing). They are Lactobacillus, Listeria monocytogenes and Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae.
- Irregular rods are pleomorphic and stain unevenly: Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium (formerly Propionibacterium), Mycobacterium, Actinomyces and Nocardia. These are then sorted by whether they are acid-fast and whether they are filamentous. Corynebacterium and Mycobacterium share mycolic acids in the wall.

cards.t: Bacillus vs Clostridium: spore position, oxygen and what they cause
q: what is the difference between Bacillus and Clostridium
where are the spores in Bacillus and Clostridium
which spore-formers are anaerobes
cards.x:
Both are Gram-positive, spore-forming rods, but nearly everything else differs.
- Bacillus: the spore sits in the center of the cell (a diagnostic feature). Aerobic (or facultatively anaerobic) and catalase positive. Mostly saprobic (feeding on dead matter), with soil as the main habitat. Versatile in breaking down complex macromolecules. It makes antibiotics such as bacitracin. Only two species matter medically: B. anthracis and B. cereus.
- Clostridium: the spore sits at the end of the cell (in Clostridium tetani it swells that end into a drumstick or tennis racket shape). Spores form only under anaerobic conditions. Anaerobic and catalase negative. About 120 species, with spores in soil, skin, intestine and vagina. They act as opportunistic pathogens. Their products include organic acids, alcohols and exotoxins that are among the most toxic substances on earth. Infections are of two types: wound and tissue infections, and food intoxications.

cards.t: Bacillus anthracis: why it matters and its capsule
q: what is Bacillus anthracis
why is anthrax a bioterrorism concern
why is Bacillus anthracis important in the history of microbiology
cards.x:
Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax, a zoonotic infection (spread from animals to people). It is a large, block-shaped rod that grows in chains with central spores. It is historically important because Koch's postulates were established with it: isolate the microbe from every case, grow it in pure culture, reproduce the disease with it, and re-isolate it.

It is also a Category A priority pathogen and a potential bioterrorism weapon; an accidental release from a Soviet bioweapon facility in 1979 was highly fatal. One of its defenses is a polypeptide capsule, which makes the cell hard for phagocytes to engulf.

cards.t: The three-part anthrax exotoxin
q: how does the anthrax toxin work
what does lethal factor do
what does protective antigen do
cards.x:
The anthrax exotoxin works as a team of three parts.
- Protective antigen binds host cells and creates a receptor site for the other two components, a bit like a docking port.
- Edema factor impairs phagocytosis and inhibits production of tumor necrosis factor and interleukin 6 by monocytes.
- Lethal factor does two things depending on dose. At low levels it inhibits release of interleukin 1 and tumor necrosis factor alpha, damping the immune response. At high levels it lyses macrophages, releasing high levels of interleukin 1, tumor necrosis factor alpha and nitric oxide.

The excessive release of those cytokines can trigger a massive inflammatory response and the shock cascade, like septic shock.

cards.t: Forms of anthrax: cutaneous, injection, pulmonary, gastrointestinal
q: what are the forms of anthrax
which form of anthrax is most deadly
what does cutaneous anthrax look like
cards.x:
Anthrax takes different forms depending on how the spores get in.
- Cutaneous (about 95% of human cases): spores enter through cuts, germinate and grow. A painless papule rapidly becomes an ulcer surrounded by vesicles and finally a black necrotic eschar.
- Injection: from contaminated heroin. Like cutaneous, but the infection is in deep muscle, so it spreads faster and is harder to recognize and treat.
- Pulmonary (woolsorters' disease), the most deadly: inhaled spores from infected animal products or soil. Alveolar macrophages engulf the spores and the exotoxins kill the macrophages en masse, causing cough, fever, chest pain, then edema, capillary thrombosis and shock. Untreated, it is nearly always fatal within about three days of symptoms.
- Gastrointestinal: from eating meat from an infected animal, with mouth and esophageal ulcers, or sepsis if the large intestine is invaded.

Meningitis can complicate any form, in up to half of pulmonary cases.

cards.t: Anthrax treatment and vaccine
q: how is anthrax treated
who gets the anthrax vaccine
how are livestock protected from anthrax
cards.x:
Anthrax is treated with antibiotics. Pulmonary anthrax is also treated with antitoxin to neutralize the toxins.

For prevention, livestock are protected with live spores and toxoid. The human vaccine, Biothrax, is a purified toxoid. It is given to people in high-risk occupations and to military personnel, but not to anyone under 18 or over 65. The current schedule is five intramuscular doses with annual boosters. After an exposure it is given as a three-dose series together with antibiotics. A second, adjuvanted anthrax vaccine was licensed in 2023 for use after exposure. Biothrax's side effects have prompted research into alternative vaccines.

cards.t: Bacillus cereus: food poisoning and welder's anthrax
q: what does Bacillus cereus cause
why is rice a risk for Bacillus cereus
what is welder's anthrax
cards.x:
Bacillus cereus is most commonly a foodborne illness, and its spores are very commonly airborne and dustborne. It grows in rice, potatoes and meat, and the spores survive cooking and reheating, so the real risk is cooked food left out before it is refrigerated.

Symptoms come from exotoxins. The diarrheal form is caused by a large protein; the emetic (vomiting) form by a small, heat-stable peptide. The illness lasts about 24 hours and has no treatment.

It can also cause severe eye infections, progressive pneumonia and post-surgical infections, and rare sepsis traced to contaminated alcohol prep pads. Welder's anthrax is a recently recognized disease of metal workers in which anthrax toxins are produced by Bacillus cereus; metal fume inhalation may predispose to it.

cards.t: How gas gangrene develops (Clostridium perfringens)
q: what is gas gangrene
why does gas gangrene need dead tissue
why is gas gangrene a mixed infection
cards.x:
Gas gangrene is a deep wound infection by anaerobes. Clostridium perfringens is the most common cause (C. novyi, C. septicum and others can also cause it). The spores live in soil and in human skin, intestine and vagina. About 90% of contaminated wounds carry the bacteria, but only about 2% develop myonecrosis (muscle death). That shows how much host factors matter.

The bacteria are not highly invasive. They need damaged, dead tissue and anaerobic conditions, which stimulate spore germination, vegetative growth and release of exotoxins. Fermentation of muscle carbohydrates forms the gas and destroys more tissue. It is a mixed infection because aerobic bacteria in the wound use up the oxygen. That produces the low oxygen tension the anaerobes need.

Predisposing wounds: surgical incisions, compound fractures, diabetic ulcers, septic abortions, puncture wounds and gunshot wounds.

cards.t: Clostridium perfringens toxins, and cellulitis vs myonecrosis
q: what toxins does Clostridium perfringens make
what is the difference between anaerobic cellulitis and myonecrosis
how does Clostridium perfringens spread through tissue
cards.x:
Clostridium perfringens makes at least 17 toxins. One ruptures red blood cells and causes edema and tissue destruction, and another destroys white blood cells. It also makes enzymes, collagenase, hyaluronidase and deoxyribonuclease, that break down connective tissue and let the infection spread.

How far it goes defines the form:
- Anaerobic cellulitis: gas and tissue damage, but the infection stays localized.
- True myonecrosis: the local infection leads to spreading tissue damage with fever, tachycardia (fast heart rate) and blackened necrotic tissue.

cards.t: Treating and preventing gas gangrene (debridement, hyperbaric oxygen)
q: how is gas gangrene treated
why is hyperbaric oxygen used
can gas gangrene be prevented by a vaccine
cards.x:
Treatment attacks the dead tissue and the anaerobe together. Surgeons remove diseased tissue (debridement), which is difficult if the infection is intestinal, and amputation may be needed. Large doses of antibiotics are given, along with hyperbaric oxygen, which floods the tissue with oxygen and inhibits the anaerobe.

Prevention is immediate cleansing of dirty wounds, deep wounds, compound fractures and infected incisions. No vaccine is available.

cards.t: Clostridium perfringens food poisoning vs botulism
q: how does Clostridium perfringens food poisoning differ from botulism
which foods cause Clostridium perfringens food poisoning
where is the perfringens toxin produced in food poisoning
cards.x:
The two clostridial food poisonings are opposites in severity. Clostridium botulinum causes a rare but severe intoxication, usually from home-canned food. Clostridium perfringens causes a mild intestinal illness but is a very common food poisoning.

For perfringens, the foods most commonly involved are meat, fish and undercooked vegetables. Spores survive cooking that was not thorough enough, then germinate and multiply, especially if the food is unrefrigerated. After the food is eaten, the toxin is produced in the intestine. It acts on epithelial cells and causes acute abdominal pain, diarrhea and nausea, with rapid recovery.

cards.t: How tetanus toxin causes muscle spasm (lockjaw)
q: how does tetanus cause muscle spasms
what does tetanospasmin block
how does tetanus differ from botulism
cards.x:
Tetanus (lockjaw) is a neuromuscular disease caused by Clostridium tetani, a strict anaerobe that lives in soil and the intestines of animals. It needs low oxygen to germinate its spores and make toxin.

The neurotoxin tetanospasmin enters at motor nerve endings and acts on the spinal inhibitory neurons. Those neurons normally keep muscles in check by releasing the inhibitory transmitters gamma-aminobutyric acid and glycine. The toxin blocks that release. With the brakes off, muscles contract uncontrollably. This causes the fixed grin of risus sardonicus and arching spasms, because opposing muscles contract together. Death is most often from respiratory failure, as spasm of the breathing muscles and larynx stops effective breathing.

Compare botulism, where the block is at the neuromuscular junction itself and the paralysis is flaccid, not spastic.

cards.t: Tetanus: how it starts, incubation, treatment and prevention
q: how do people get tetanus
what does tetanus antitoxin do
how often is a tetanus booster needed
cards.x:
Tetanus is most common in older patients, intravenous drug users and newborns in developing countries. Spores usually enter through accidental puncture wounds, and also through burns, umbilical stumps (neonatal tetanus), frostbite and crushed body parts. The rust on a nail has nothing to do with it; the danger is the puncture wound. Incubation is 4 to 10 days, and the shorter the incubation, the more serious the disease. Delayed care, a short incubation and head wounds worsen the outlook.

Treatment is aimed at the toxin and the infection and at maintaining homeostasis: antitoxin (human tetanus immune globulin) inactivates circulating toxin but does not counteract toxin already bound, antibiotics treat the infection, and muscle relaxants control the spasms. Prevention is a vaccine, with a booster every 10 years.

cards.t: How botulism happens: home canning and botulin
q: how does botulism cause paralysis
why are home-canned foods a botulism risk
what does botulin do at the neuromuscular junction
cards.x:
Botulism is an intoxication associated with inadequate food preservation. Clostridium botulinum is a spore-forming anaerobe of soil and water. The risk is highest with low-acid, home-canned foods such as green beans and corn, though meats, fish and dairy can carry it, and rarely commercial foods.

The chain of events: spores are on the food when it is gathered. If reliable temperature and pressure are not achieved when canning, the air is evacuated but the spores remain. The anaerobic conditions favor germination and growth, and the toxin, botulin, is released. It is carried to neuromuscular junctions, where it blocks release of acetylcholine, the transmitter muscles need to contract. With no acetylcholine, the muscle cannot contract, so the paralysis is flaccid (limp).

cards.t: Botulism symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and prevention
q: what are the symptoms of botulism
how is botulism treated
how do you prevent botulism from canned food
cards.x:
Botulism begins with double or blurred vision, difficulty swallowing and dizziness, sometimes with nausea and vomiting. It then produces descending muscular paralysis (starting at the top of the body and moving down) and respiratory compromise. Mortality has fallen because ventilators support breathing through the paralysis.

Diagnosis is by finding the toxin in the food, intestinal contents or feces. Treatment is antitoxin with cardiac and respiratory support. Infant botulism is treated differently, with botulism immune globulin.

Prevention is proper preserving and handling of canned foods, using sodium nitrite, salt or vinegar as preservatives. Discard bulging cans, and boil home-bottled foods for at least 10 minutes. Boiling works because the toxin is sensitive to heat even though the spore is not.

cards.t: Forms of botulism: infant, foodborne, wound, iatrogenic
q: what is infant botulism
why should infants not eat honey
what are the types of botulism
cards.x:
Botulism has several forms, depending on where the toxin comes from.
- Infant botulism, the most common form (up to 80% of cases each year): ingested spores germinate and release toxin in the infant gut, because the immature infant digestive system lets them meet the anaerobic conditions they need. It causes flaccid paralysis called floppy baby syndrome and is associated with honey or homemade baby food.
- Foodborne: eating toxin made in improperly preserved, usually home-canned, food.
- Wound: spores enter a wound and cause the food poisoning symptoms; seen in intravenous drug users, often with black tar heroin.
- Iatrogenic (caused by medical treatment): cosmetic or therapeutic procedures using botulinum toxin cause systemic intoxication.
- Intestinal colonization: a person over age 1 harbors the toxin in the intestinal tract.

Floppy baby syndrome is the flaccid opposite of neonatal tetanus, where the newborn is rigid and arched: botulism means no muscle tone and limbs hanging limp.

cards.t: Clostridioides difficile: how antibiotics lead to pseudomembranous colitis
q: how does Clostridioides difficile cause colitis
why do antibiotics cause C difficile infection
what is pseudomembranous colitis
cards.x:
Clostridioides difficile is a normal resident of the colon in low numbers and is relatively non-invasive. Its name changed from Clostridium after ribonucleic acid sequencing placed it in its own genus.

The problem starts with broad-spectrum antibiotics, which kill the other bacteria and let C. difficile overgrow. It then produces enterotoxins that damage the intestines. Disease ranges from antibiotic-associated (pseudomembranous) colitis to toxic megacolon and perforation of the colon. The course is watery diarrhea, fever, loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal pain and tenderness. Then the intestinal lining becomes necrotic and sloughs off as the pseudomembrane (the raised yellow-white plaques), and the wall can perforate.

It is a major cause of diarrhea in hospitals and increasingly common in community-acquired diarrhea.

cards.t: Clostridioides difficile: who is at risk, and treatment and prevention
q: who is at risk for Clostridioides difficile infection
what is a fecal microbiota transplant
how is Clostridioides difficile infection managed
cards.x:
People at risk include those with recent antibiotic exposure (70% of cases used antibiotics in the prior 12 weeks), gastrointestinal surgery, long stays in healthcare settings, serious underlying illness, immunocompromise, advanced age, and use of gastric acid inhibitors such as famotidine and omeprazole. Trehalose, a sugar, is another risk factor.

Withdrawing the antimicrobial that set it off is part of managing every case. Mild cases also get fluid and electrolyte replacement. Current guidelines also treat mild cases with an oral antibiotic. For severe disease they prefer oral fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin, and metronidazole is no longer recommended. Fecal microbiota transplant gives donor cultures by colonoscope or nasogastric tube, or as capsules, to restore the normal flora. It is as much as 90% effective. Prevention is increased precautions to prevent spread.

cards.t: Lactobacillus: beneficial normal flora
q: what does Lactobacillus do
why can antibiotics lead to a vaginal yeast infection
cards.x: Lactobacillus (L. acidophilus, L. salivarius, L. fermentum) is beneficial normal flora of the intestinal and vaginal tracts. It protects by producing lactic acid, acetic acid, hydrogen peroxide and other antimicrobial substances that inhibit pathogens. Antibiotic therapy can interrupt its activity and allow a superinfection. That is an overgrowth by an opportunist. A vaginal yeast infection is an example.

cards.t: Listeria monocytogenes: how it survives and hides from antibody
q: how does Listeria avoid the immune system
why is Listeria a problem in refrigerated food
what are the features of Listeria monocytogenes
cards.x:
Listeria monocytogenes is a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming rod, ranging from coccobacilli to long filaments, with 1 to 4 flagella and no capsule. It is hardy: resistant to cold, salt, pH extremes and bile. Calling it heat resistant only means it tolerates warmth better than most bacteria. Pasteurization and cooking still kill it. Its primary reservoir is soil and water, plus animal intestines.

Its clever trick is staying out of reach of antibody. It induces its own uptake by phagocytosis and escapes the vacuole. It multiplies in the cytoplasm of the host cell and passes directly into the neighboring cell without ever leaving the cells. That lets it avoid the humoral (antibody) immune system.

cards.t: Listeriosis: food sources, who is at risk, diagnosis and prevention
q: how do people get listeriosis
who is most at risk for listeriosis
does refrigeration stop Listeria
cards.x:
Listeria contaminates foods and grows during refrigeration. Most listeriosis comes from dairy products, poultry and meat; it has been found in 12% of ground beef and 15% of chicken tested, and the most recent outbreak was dairy.

In healthy adults the illness is often mild or subclinical, with fever, diarrhea and sore throat. In immunocompromised patients, fetuses and neonates it affects the brain and meninges, with fetal loss and newborn deaths.

Diagnosis by culture requires a lengthy cold enrichment process; rapid tests use enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, immunofluorescence and nucleic acid analysis. Prevention is pasteurization and cooking, because refrigeration does not stop it.

cards.t: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (erysipeloid)
q: what is Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae
how do people get erysipeloid
cards.x: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae is a Gram-positive rod found in animals and the environment, and its primary reservoir is the tonsils of healthy pigs. It enters through skin abrasions and produces erysipeloid, dark red lesions on the hand. Rarely it causes septicemia or endocarditis. Pigs are vaccinated.

cards.t: Corynebacterium diphtheriae and the two stages of diphtheria
q: what is diphtheria
what is the pseudomembrane in diphtheria
what does diphtheria toxin do to the body
cards.x:
Corynebacterium diphtheriae is an irregular rod: pleomorphic cells in a palisade arrangement (rods lying side by side like a fence, rather than end to end in a chain) with granules. Healthy human carriers are the reservoir, so the potential for diphtheria is always present, though respiratory diphtheria is rare in the United States. It spreads by respiratory droplets and affects non-immunized children in crowded, unsanitary conditions. The disease can be respiratory (pharyngeal, tonsillar, laryngeal, nasal) or cutaneous, which is most common in the tropics.

It unfolds in two stages. Stage 1 is local infection: upper respiratory inflammation with sore throat, nausea, vomiting and swollen lymph nodes. The pseudomembrane, formed from solidified inflammatory fluid, is the telltale sign and can cause asphyxiation. Stage 2 is toxemia: diphtherotoxin targets the heart (myocarditis, abnormal electrocardiogram) and the nerves (muscle weakness, paralysis).

cards.t: Diagnosing, treating and preventing diphtheria
q: how is diphtheria diagnosed
what does diphtheria antitoxin do
when is the diphtheria vaccine given
cards.x:
Diagnosis rests on the pseudomembrane and swelling, a stain with alkaline methylene blue, the conditions and history, and a serological assay.

Treatment is antitoxin made in horse serum (used since the 1890s) plus antibiotics. The antitoxin is not usually given in non-respiratory cases. It neutralizes circulating toxin but not toxin that is already bound.

Prevention is a toxoid vaccine series, given at 6 to 8 weeks, 15 months and school age, with boosters.

cards.t: Cutibacterium acnes: acne and implant infections
q: what causes acne
why are Cutibacterium acnes implant infections hard to diagnose and treat
what is Cutibacterium acnes
cards.x:
Cutibacterium acnes (the genus Propionibacterium is now Cutibacterium) is a Gram-positive rod. It is aerotolerant or anaerobic, slow growing (more than 6 days) and nontoxigenic. It is a common resident of the pilosebaceous glands (hair follicles with oil glands). It causes acne through inflammatory mediators, not a toxin.

It also causes chronic invasive, implant, endovascular and central nervous system shunt infections, because it forms a biofilm on prosthetics. The biofilm raises its tolerance to antibiotics and immune defense. Diagnosis is hard because it grows so slowly. Fluid from an infected site may show nothing for days, so prolonged incubation under strict anaerobic conditions is needed. Treatment may require removing the hardware, aggressive debridement and prolonged antibiotics, often 3 to 6 months.

cards.t: Mycobacteria: acid-fast stain and how they resist destruction
q: why are mycobacteria acid-fast
what is cord factor
why do mycobacteria Gram stain poorly
cards.x:
Mycobacteria are acid-fast bacilli: Gram-positive irregular rods whose walls contain mycolic acids and waxes. That waxy wall is why the acid-fast stain (carbol fuchsin) needs heat to drive it in, and why they Gram stain poorly. They are strict aerobes, produce catalase, form no capsules, flagella or spores, and grow slowly. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria are a problem in the immunosuppressed.

Their virulence is unusual. They have no exotoxins or enzymes that contribute to infectiousness. Instead, complex waxes and cord factor prevent destruction by lysosomes and macrophages, so the bacillus survives inside the cells meant to kill it.

cards.t: Tuberculosis spread, latent infection vs active disease
q: what is the difference between latent tuberculosis and active tuberculosis
how is tuberculosis spread
who is predisposed to tuberculosis
cards.x:
Tuberculosis spreads by airborne respiratory droplets, and the bacillus is very resistant, with an infectious dose of only about 10 cells. About a third of the world carries it, and the highest United States rate is in recent immigrants. Poor nutrition, a weakened immune system, poor access to care, lung damage and genetics predispose to it.

Infection is not the same as disease: only 5 to 10% of infected people develop clinical disease. Inactive (latent) tuberculosis is not contagious, can be detected by a blood or skin test, and may activate at any time. Untreated disease progresses slowly and mostly stays in the lungs.

cards.t: Primary, secondary and disseminated tuberculosis
q: what happens in primary tuberculosis
what is a tubercle
what is reactivation tuberculosis
cards.x:
Tuberculosis passes through stages.
- Primary: the bacilli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages and multiply inside them. After 3 to 4 weeks the immune system attacks, building tubercles: granulomas with a central core of bacilli surrounded by white blood cells. If the center breaks down into necrotic caseous (cheese-like) lesions, they gradually heal by calcification. This stimulates a cell-mediated response.
- Secondary (reactivation or reinfection): if the patient does not recover, the bacilli reactivate. Tubercles expand and drain into the bronchial tubes and upper respiratory tract, causing violent coughing, greenish or bloody sputum, fever, anorexia, weight loss and fatigue. It was called consumption because patients wasted away.
- Disseminated (extrapulmonary): bacilli spread to regional lymph nodes, kidneys, long bones, the genital tract, brain and meninges. Tuberculous meningitis is grave even when treated.

cards.t: Testing for tuberculosis: Mantoux, blood test, false results, sputum
q: how does the Mantoux test work
what can cause a false positive tuberculin test
how is active tuberculosis diagnosed
cards.x:
Two tests detect exposure. The Mantoux (tuberculin) test places purified protein derivative into the skin. It is read at 48 to 72 hours for induration (a firm raised area), interpreted by size and the patient's population factors. It is read that late because it is a delayed, type IV reaction. Once positive, it stays positive because of memory cells. The QuantiFERON Gold blood test incubates blood with mycobacterial proteins and measures release of gamma interferon.

False positives happen after prior bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccine or infection by other Mycobacterium species. False negatives happen too early in infection, or with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome or other immunosuppression, where the patient cannot mount the response.

To diagnose active disease: acid-fast stain of sputum (Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorescent), laboratory cultivation, nucleic acid probes, and chest X-ray for tubercles.

cards.t: Treating and preventing tuberculosis
q: how long is tuberculosis treated
what vaccine is used for tuberculosis
who gets preventive therapy for tuberculosis
cards.x:
Tuberculosis treatment takes months and always needs more than one drug; a one-pill regimen combines three. Drug-susceptible tuberculosis is standardly treated for six months: four drugs for two months, then two drugs for four. Preventive treatment is given to those at risk or latently infected, and the preferred latent regimens are now shorter rifamycin-based courses, with nine months of isoniazid as an alternative.

The vaccine used in other countries is the attenuated bacille Calmette-Guérin strain of Mycobacterium bovis.

cards.t: Mycobacterium leprae: growth, spread and course of leprosy
q: what is leprosy
why are armadillos used to study Mycobacterium leprae
how does leprosy damage nerves
cards.x:
Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic disease that begins in the skin and mucous membranes and progresses into the nerves. Mycobacterium leprae is a strict parasite: it has not been grown on artificial media or in tissue culture, so armadillos are used. It is the slowest growing of all species and multiplies inside host cells in large packets called globi.

How it spreads is not fully verified; zoonotic transmission from armadillos is possible. It is not highly virulent: health, living conditions and possibly a genetic marker influence susceptibility. Most Florida cases are in Central Florida, along the I-4 corridor.

Macrophages engulf the bacilli, but a weakened macrophage or slow T cell response may not kill them. Incubation is 2 to 5 years. Untreated, the bacilli grow slowly in skin macrophages and in the Schwann cells of peripheral nerves.

cards.t: Tuberculoid vs lepromatous leprosy
k: T helper 1 vs T helper 2 leprosy
q: what is the difference between tuberculoid and lepromatous leprosy
why is lepromatous leprosy more severe
which T helper response favors each form of leprosy
cards.x:
Leprosy has two polar forms (several intermediate forms exist), and the type of T helper response tends to favor one form or the other.
- Tuberculoid: a T helper 1 response, with normal T cell responsiveness to the bacillus. Low to undetectable numbers of bacilli, low infectivity, granulomas and local inflammation. Lesions are shallow and asymmetrical, with nerve damage and local loss of pain reception.
- Lepromatous: a T helper 2 response, with low or absent T cell responsiveness. Because that response fails, the bacilli grow freely in macrophages: florid growth, high infectivity and hypergammaglobulinemia. Lesions are deeply nodular, severely disfiguring the face and extremities, with widespread dissemination.

cards.t: Leprosy diagnosis, treatment and prevention
q: how is leprosy diagnosed
what is the feather test
how long is leprosy treated
cards.x:
Leprosy is diagnosed from symptoms, microscopy of lesions and history. The clues are numbness in the hands and feet, loss of heat and cold sensitivity, muscle weakness, thickened earlobes and a chronic stuffy nose. Acid-fast bacilli in skin lesions, nasal discharge and tissue also point to it. Where care is scarce, the feather test checks skin sensation: can the patient feel a feather?

Treatment is long-term combined therapy. Older United States practice was about 6 months for tuberculoid leprosy and up to 2 years for lepromatous leprosy, followed by extended single-drug treatment. The current United States program uses about 12 months for tuberculoid and about 2 years for lepromatous leprosy. The World Health Organization now gives all three drugs for both forms (6 and 12 months). Prevention is constant surveillance of high-risk populations. Bacille Calmette-Guérin has limited efficacy. A subunit vaccine is in trials.

cards.t: Actinomyces israelii and Actinomyces viscosus
q: what does Actinomyces israelii cause
where does Actinomyces live in the body
how is actinomycosis treated
cards.x:
Actinomyces and Nocardia are nonmotile filamentous (thread-like) bacteria related to the mycobacteria. They may cause chronic infection of skin and soft tissue.

Actinomyces israelii is a normally harmless resident of the oral cavity, digestive tract and genital tract. It causes a chronic, hard-to-diagnose infection when it gets into deeper tissues.
- Cervicofacial disease is a complication of oral infection.
- Thoracic disease is a necrotizing lung disorder.
- Abdominal disease is a complication of a burst appendix, gunshot wounds or ulcers.
- Uterine disease is a complication of intrauterine devices.

It is treated surgically and with antibiotics. Actinomyces viscosus causes dental caries and some cases of endocarditis.

cards.t: Nocardia and nocardiosis (pulmonary, cutaneous, mycetoma)
k: Nocardia lung infection looks like tuberculosis
q: what does Nocardia cause
how is pulmonary nocardiosis similar to tuberculosis
what is mycetoma
which Nocardia species causes lung disease and which causes mycetoma
cards.x: Nocardia causes nocardiosis, which can be pulmonary, cutaneous or subcutaneous. Pulmonary nocardiosis resembles tuberculosis. The lesions may extend through the chest wall and disseminate to the brain and kidneys. Pulmonary nocardiosis is mainly caused by the Nocardia asteroides complex. Nocardia brasiliensis is the classic cause of cutaneous disease and mycetoma, a granulomatous inflammatory response in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Treating with cephalosporins alone is incomplete; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual first-line drug.

cards.t: How the spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli are acquired
q: how is Bacillus anthracis transmitted
how do people get Clostridium tetani
how is Clostridioides difficile acquired
cards.x:
Each spore-former has its own route in.
- Bacillus anthracis: a zoonosis from spores. Through a cut (cutaneous), inhaled from animal wool or soil (pulmonary), eaten in meat from an infected animal (gastrointestinal), or injected with contaminated heroin (injection).
- Bacillus cereus: food such as rice, potatoes and meat, from airborne and dustborne spores that survive cooking and reheating; also contaminated alcohol prep pads at injection sites.
- Clostridium perfringens: spores from soil, skin, intestine or vagina in deep, dirty wounds with dead tissue; undercooked meat and fish for food poisoning.
- Clostridium tetani: spores from soil through puncture wounds, burns, frostbite, crush injuries and the newborn's umbilical stump.
- Clostridium botulinum: preformed toxin in low-acid, home-canned foods; swallowed spores in infants (honey, homemade baby food); spores in wounds (black tar heroin); medical use of the toxin.

Clostridioides difficile is different: overgrowth of the patient's own colonic resident after broad-spectrum antibiotics, with spread in hospitals.

cards.t: How the non-spore-forming Gram-positive bacilli are acquired
q: how is Listeria monocytogenes transmitted
how is Corynebacterium diphtheriae spread
how does Cutibacterium acnes cause implant infection
cards.x:
For the non-spore-formers, the route depends on the microbe.
- Listeria monocytogenes: from soil, water and animal intestines into food such as dairy, poultry and meat, where it grows during refrigeration.
- Corynebacterium diphtheriae: respiratory droplets from healthy carriers or patients.
- Cutibacterium acnes: the patient's own skin resident, onto implants and prosthetics.
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis: airborne respiratory droplets, with an infectious dose of about 10 cells.
- Mycobacterium leprae: not fully verified, possibly zoonotic from armadillos; it seems to need prolonged close contact.

Actinomyces israelii comes from the patient's own oral, digestive or genital tract reaching deeper tissue. Examples are oral infection, burst appendix, gunshot wounds, ulcers and intrauterine devices. Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae comes from pigs through skin abrasions.

cards.t: Infant botulism treatment, and honey
q: how is infant botulism treated
when should honey be avoided in babies
are antibiotics used for infant botulism
cards.x:
Infant botulism is treated with botulism immune globulin. Antibiotics are not recommended for it. Penicillin applies to wound botulism, after antitoxin and debridement.

Honey is a source of botulism spores, and the standard rule is no honey before 12 months of age.

cards.t: Irregular rods: which are catalase positive and have mycolic acids
q: which irregular rods have mycolic acids
is Actinomyces catalase positive
does Cutibacterium have mycolic acids
cards.x: Not every irregular Gram-positive rod is catalase positive or has mycolic acids in its wall. Corynebacterium, Mycobacterium and Nocardia do have both. Actinomyces is catalase negative and lacks mycolic acids, and Cutibacterium lacks mycolic acids too. The pair that is worth remembering: Corynebacterium and Mycobacterium share mycolic acids in the wall.

cards.t: Antibiotic resistance and why we need novel therapies
q: why do we need new antimicrobial therapies
what drives antibiotic resistance
what is antibiotic resistance
cards.x:
Antibiotic resistance means an antibiotic no longer kills or controls the bacteria it was meant for. It belongs to the bacteria, not the patient: an allergy is the patient reacting to the drug, while resistance is the drug no longer working on the organism.

Resistance follows use, which is why it keeps spreading even with over 100 antibiotics on the market. Penicillin, vancomycin and azithromycin each met resistant bacteria within a few years to about two decades of coming into wide use. Four things feed it:
- overuse of antibiotics in agriculture, in plants and animals
- clinically inappropriate prescriptions
- antibiotic prophylaxis, meaning antibiotics given to reduce infection risk "when possible"
- patients not finishing their course, such as stopping early or leaving against medical advice
That is the push behind novel therapies such as fecal microbiota transplant and phages.

cards.t: Antimicrobial stewardship and its cycle
q: what is antimicrobial stewardship
what are the steps of the stewardship cycle
how does stewardship reduce resistance
cards.x:
Antimicrobial stewardship is the answer to inappropriate prescribing: educating clinicians and patients so antibiotics are used only when they are actually needed.

It works as a loop. First diagnose a bacterial disease, because antibiotics do nothing for viruses. Then ask whether a non-antibiotic option could prevent, control or treat it. If not, use antimicrobials judiciously. Finally re-evaluate whether they are still needed, which brings you back to the start. Think of it as a checkpoint before, during and after every prescription, so no course starts without a reason or runs on without a review.

cards.t: When antibiotics are and are not needed
q: does green mucus mean I need antibiotics
do sore throats need antibiotics
do antibiotics work on viruses
cards.x:
Antibiotics are life-saving drugs, but they treat only bacterial infections, so they do nothing for a viral illness. These are the points patients are told:
- most sore throats do not need an antibiotic
- some ear infections do not need one either
- green mucus is not a sign that an antibiotic is needed
- every prescription drug carries risks, such as allergy, rash and diarrhea
So the question before prescribing is not whether the patient feels sick, but whether a bacterial infection is likely. Resistance follows use, so an antibiotic given without a need adds risks and feeds resistance without any benefit.

cards.t: Superbugs: the drug-resistant bacteria to know
q: what are superbugs
which bacteria are superbugs
which bacteria top the lists of hospital-acquired infections
cards.x:
Superbugs are the bacteria best known for antibiotic resistance. The list includes methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, toxigenic Escherichia coli and Clostridioides difficile.

A related group of pathogens, which has its own acronym, tops the lists of organisms causing nosocomial, meaning hospital-acquired, infections. Resistance is the common thread, and it is exactly the problem novel therapies are meant to get around.

cards.t: Disk diffusion (Kirby-Bauer) testing
q: how does a Kirby-Bauer test work
what does the zone of inhibition mean
how do you read a disk diffusion plate
cards.x:
Disk diffusion, also called the Kirby-Bauer test, shows which antibiotics work against a particular organism. White paper disks treated with different antibiotics are placed on an agar plate already spread with the bacteria. Each antibiotic diffuses out into the agar around its disk.

The circular clear area around a disk is the zone of inhibition. A wide clear ring means the antibiotic stopped that organism growing; bacteria growing right up to the disk mean the drug had little effect. Think of each disk as a little fence: the bigger the empty yard around it, the better it keeps the bacteria out.

cards.t: Antibiograms and their limitations
q: what is an antibiogram
what is an antibiogram used for
what are the limitations of an antibiogram
cards.x:
An antibiogram is a profile of antimicrobial susceptibility, given as percentages: how often an organism is susceptible to each drug. Clinicians use it to guide empiric therapy, the choice made before a patient's own results are back. For example, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is far less often susceptible to ciprofloxacin and erythromycin than methicillin-susceptible strains, while both are fully susceptible to vancomycin.

It is a population summary, so it has blind spots:
- it leaves out the minimum inhibitory concentration (the lowest drug concentration that stops growth)
- it does not consider the patient's risk factors
- it has no data on synergy when drugs are combined
- the numbers may apply only to a single hospital within a health system

cards.t: Empiric antibiotic therapy
q: what is empiric therapy
when do you start antibiotics before cultures
what is empiric therapy based on
cards.x:
Empiric therapy means starting an antibiotic before the cultures are confirmed or other diagnostic results are available. It is common in human and veterinary medicine, especially for critically ill or emergent patients who cannot safely wait.

The choice rests on prior clinical experience and/or antibiograms. Once results arrive, the treatment is adjusted, for example from intravenous to oral. Quick way to tell it from prophylaxis: empiric therapy treats an infection the patient probably has; prophylaxis tries to prevent one they do not have yet.

cards.t: Antimicrobial prophylaxis: when it is justified
q: when are antibiotics given to prevent infection
who needs dental antibiotic prophylaxis
why do implants get infected
cards.x:
Prophylaxis means giving an antimicrobial to prevent an infection rather than treat one. It is kept for special circumstances:
- prosthetic implants and devices, which are prone to biofilm formation
- before surgery, to reduce post-operative surgical site infections
- immunocompromised patients, such as those with human immunodeficiency virus infection, on cancer chemotherapy, or on immunosuppressive therapy for an organ transplant
- contacts of an infected patient, to prevent transmission, for example in tuberculosis, meningitis or pertussis
- high-risk traumatic injuries such as animal bites or penetrating brain injury
For dental and other invasive procedures, many dentists now limit it to a few high-risk scenarios, such as a prosthetic heart valve or a history of endocarditis.

cards.t: Direct and indirect adverse effects of antimicrobials
q: what are the direct and indirect adverse effects of antibiotics
is C. diff a direct or indirect effect
what can go wrong with antibiotics
cards.x:
Every antimicrobial course carries costs, and they come in two kinds.

Direct effects come from the drug itself: allergy, which can be life-threatening; acute or chronic toxicity, such as kidney or liver toxicity; drug-drug interactions; and therapeutic failure.

Indirect effects work through other microbes: effects on the commensal (normal) flora of humans or animals, including Clostridioides difficile infection; a greater chance of infection with drug-resistant pathogens; and effects on environmental flora, such as antibiotics in the food or water supply. Clostridioides difficile infection is what happens when an antibiotic clears the commensal flora, which makes it the bridge to fecal microbiota transplant, the therapy that puts that flora back.

cards.t: Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
q: what is fecal microbiota transplant
what is FMT used for
how does a fecal transplant treat C. diff
cards.x:
Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) gives a patient screened donor stool to realign their gastrointestinal microflora, sometimes nicknamed "the power of poop". It is far from new: it has been used for centuries in human and animal medicine, including old Chinese recipes for "yellow soup", and veterinarians call it transfaunation.

Its established use is preventing recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, which causes about 500,000 cases a year and about 30,000 deaths in the United States alone. Instead of adding another antibiotic, the transplant works by putting a donor's gut microflora in place.

cards.t: How fecal transplant is given and how donors are screened
q: how is a fecal transplant given
what are stool donors screened for
what is a stool bank
cards.x:
Fecal microbiota transplant is given by nasogastric tube, colonoscopy or enema, using screened donor stool. Stool banks make it more accessible.

Donor screening is similar to blood bank screening, to reduce the risk from blood-borne and other pathogens. Donors are screened for:
- human immunodeficiency virus
- hepatitis A, B and C
- syphilis
- Clostridioides difficile
- the parasites Giardia and Cryptosporidium

cards.t: Bacteriophages and why therapy needs lytic phages
q: what is a bacteriophage
why does phage therapy use lytic phages
what are the parts of a phage
cards.x:
Bacteriophages, or phages, are very small viruses that specifically attack bacteria and no other type of cell. Like all viruses they carry DNA or RNA. A tailed phage has a head that holds its genome; a tail tube inside a sheath delivers the genome through the bacterial wall, and the baseplate and long tail fibers attach the phage to its host.

Phages replicate by one of two life cycles. In the lytic cycle the phage destroys the bacterium; in the lysogenic cycle it settles into the bacterium's genome instead. Therapy needs lytic phages with DNA, because the goal is to destroy the bacteria. As the saying goes, "the enemy of my enemy is my friend": the bacteria's own enemies, put to work for the patient.

cards.t: Phage therapy: benefits and drawbacks
q: what are the benefits of phage therapy
what are the problems with phage therapy
why must you know the organism before phage therapy
cards.x:
Phage therapy uses lytic phages to destroy a patient's infecting bacteria. Its key trait is high host specificity: phages attack specific bacteria. That cuts both ways. The idea is old: it was explored in eastern Europe in the 1920s and 1930s and abandoned in the West once antibiotics arrived.

The upside: phages could attack highly antibiotic-resistant strains, the narrow spectrum should preserve the patient's existing microbiome, side effects are potentially low-risk, they spread widely in the body after systemic administration, and they die off once their host bacteria are gone.

The downside: clinicians must know the causative organism, which can be slow and costly to identify; the optimal dose, route, frequency and duration still need to be precisely defined; gene transfer is a worry, because a phage might transfer DNA to its host cell; and no phage product is yet approved as a medicine, so investigational drug status and emergency use authorization are the ways around it.

cards.t: Corticosteroids, immunoglobulin and convalescent plasma
q: how do corticosteroids help in infection
what is convalescent plasma
what are non-antibiotic treatment options
cards.x:
Some alternatives to antibiotics do not attack the microbe at all; they work on the patient's side of the fight.

Systemic corticosteroids decrease the host's inflammatory response. They do not kill the pathogen, so their role is to calm the inflammation, not to clear the infection.

Intravenous immunoglobulin G and convalescent plasma give the patient ready-made antibodies from donors. Convalescent plasma comes specifically from people who have recovered from the infection. Quick way to keep them apart: corticosteroids turn the patient's own response down, while donor antibodies supply ready-made antibodies from someone else.

cards.t: Prebiotics versus probiotics
q: what is the difference between prebiotics and probiotics
what are examples of probiotics
where do probiotics come from
cards.x:
Probiotics are the beneficial microbes themselves; prebiotics are the food that feeds them. Think of a garden: probiotics are the seeds, prebiotics are the fertilizer.

Prebiotics are fiber-rich foods that provide nutrients to the gut microflora. Probiotics are the beneficial organisms themselves, such as Lactobacillus, a bacterium, and Saccharomyces, a fungus (a yeast). They are often found in fermented foods. A related point from the crowd-sourced American Gut project: the more diverse your plant intake, the more diverse your gut microbiota.

cards.t: Herbs, spices and plant essential oils as antimicrobials
q: do essential oils kill bacteria
why might spice use be heaviest in hot climates
which herbs and spices have antimicrobial properties
cards.x:
Plant essential oils show antibacterial activity in vitro, meaning in laboratory tests, but better experimental design is needed to test what that means for patients. Promising in a dish is not the same as proven in people.

One idea about why people use herbs and spices at all is that some kill bacteria and fungi, especially those that spoil food. If so, spice use should be heaviest where a hot climate goes with rapid food spoilage. Other hypotheses are that they season food across cultures, may provide macro- and micronutrients, and enhance taste and smell. The herbs and spices named include garlic, onion, oregano, thyme, cinnamon, cumin, ginger, cloves, rosemary and many more.

cards.t: Transduction and the phage gene-transfer concern
q: what is transduction
why is gene transfer a concern with phage therapy
is a phage injecting its DNA transduction
cards.x:
Transduction is a phage carrying bacterial genes from one bacterium to another. It is not the same as a phage injecting its own genome into a bacterium; that injection is simply how a phage infects its host.

The difference matters for phage therapy's safety question: what if the phage transfers DNA to its host bacterium? Through transduction, a phage can move genes such as toxin or resistance genes between bacteria. That is the real gene-transfer worry listed among phage therapy's concerns.

cards.t: What fecal microbiota transplant is proven for
k: fecal transplant for irritable bowel syndrome
q: is fecal transplant proven for irritable bowel syndrome
what is fecal microbiota transplant approved for
does fecal transplant work for ulcerative colitis
cards.x:
Fecal microbiota transplant is proven for one thing: preventing recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection. That is its established use, and the only one with approved products.

It is sometimes described as a successful option for irritable bowel syndrome, ulcerative colitis and chronic constipation. For those conditions, though, the evidence is limited and mixed. So if you are asked what a fecal transplant is established for, the answer is recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, not those other bowel conditions.

cards.t: Are there really no new antibiotics, and how fast does resistance appear?
q: has there been a new antibiotic in 30 years
how quickly does resistance appear after a new antibiotic
is resistance always after widespread use
cards.x:
The claim that there has been no new major antibiotic in 30 years is out of date: new agents, including new classes, have been approved since.

What does hold is the pattern that resistance followed widespread use within years. Exact dates for discovery, widespread use and first resistance differ between sources. For example, a bacterial enzyme that destroys penicillin was described in 1940, before the drug was in wide use. So remember the pattern, resistance following use, rather than any single date.

cards.t: Descriptive vs analytic epidemiology
q: what is the difference between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
what does descriptive epidemiology do
which study designs are analytic
cards.x:
Descriptive epidemiology looks at how a disease is spread through a population, by time, place and person. It forms hypotheses and spots associations, and its typical design is the community health survey (also called a cross-sectional or descriptive study). Analytic epidemiology goes a step further: it tests a specific hypothesis about whether a particular cause leads to a disease, by relating the exposure of interest to the outcome of interest. Its goal is a cause-effect relationship, and its typical designs are cohort, case-control and experimental studies.

Descriptive comes first, because you have to understand the basic picture before you test a cause. Quick way to keep the triads straight: descriptive uses person, place, time; analytic uses host, agent, environment.

cards.t: The descriptive triad: person, place, time
q: what are person, place and time in epidemiology
what is a secular trend
what are the time trends in descriptive epidemiology
cards.x:
Descriptive epidemiology organizes a disease picture around three questions: who, where and when.

- Person: age, gender, socio-economic status (education, occupation, income), marital status, ethnicity, race and genetic profile, and behavior and habits.
- Place: is it geographically restricted or widespread (outbreak, epidemic, pandemic)? Think about climate effects, urban versus rural settings, links to the water or food supply, and whether there is one cluster or several.
- Time: is the pattern changing or stable? Clustered (epidemic) or evenly spread (endemic)?

Time trends come in four kinds: point source (localized and stationary), propagated (a spreading infection, which may be extended), seasonal, and secular. A secular trend is how often a disease occurs over a prolonged period, usually years.

cards.t: The analytic triad: host, agent, environment
q: what are host, agent and environment
what counts as an agent in epidemiology
what is the role of a vector, vehicle or reservoir
cards.x:
Analytic epidemiology assesses three things: the agent, the host and the environment.

- Agent: the thing that can cause harm. It can be biological (microorganisms), physical (temperature, radiation, trauma), chemical (acids, alkalis, poisons, tobacco), environmental (nutrients in the diet, allergens), or even psychological experiences.
- Host: the one affected, including genetic endowment, immunologic status, personal characteristics and personal behavior. In vector-borne diseases there are definitive and intermediate hosts.
- Environment: living conditions (housing, crowding, water supply, refuse, sewage), atmosphere and climate, and the modes of communication, meaning whatever brings host and agent together, such as a vector, vehicle or reservoir.

cards.t: John Snow's Golden Square cholera outbreak (descriptive)
q: what did John Snow do in the Golden Square outbreak
what is a spot map
how did Snow find the source of cholera
cards.x:
In the Golden Square outbreak in London, John Snow marked on a map where people with cholera lived and worked, and also marked the water pumps. This is now called a spot map. More cases clustered near Pump A than near pumps B or C, residents said they preferred Pump A, and households with cholera all drew from Pump A, which made it the common factor. Few cases occurred two blocks to the east, where a brewery had its own deep well and let employees take their water.

Officials were notified, the pump was closed and the outbreak ended. This is descriptive epidemiology: time, place and person pointed him to the source. Snow did it without any knowledge of microbes, showing that water could transmit cholera.

cards.t: John Snow's water company comparison (analytic)
q: how was Snow's work analytic
which water company had more cholera deaths
what did Snow's second study show
cards.x:
Snow's second study was analytic. Looking back over data from different outbreaks, he saw that the districts with the highest death rates were served by two water companies, Lambeth and Southwark and Vauxhall, both drawing from the Thames downstream from London. (Lambeth later moved its intake upstream.) He proposed that water from below London was the source and tested the idea by identifying the water source for every house with a cholera death.

The result: houses supplied only by Southwark and Vauxhall had a cholera death rate of 4.2 per 1,000 people, versus 0.5 per 1,000 for houses supplied only by Lambeth. He had a hypothesis and compared exposure to outcome, which is what makes it analytic. Koch's postulates, which proved cause and effect between microbes and disease, came later.

cards.t: Studying a noncommunicable disease: the descriptive groundwork
q: how do you study a noncommunicable disease
what are the steps of a noncommunicable disease study
cards.x:
Noncommunicable disease, meaning illness that does not spread from person to person, is studied with the same descriptive groundwork, followed by these steps in order:
1. Define the population of interest.
2. Conceptualize and create measures of exposures and health indicators.
3. Take a sample of the population.
4. Estimate measures of association between exposures and health indicators.
5. Rigorously evaluate whether the association suggests a causal one.
6. Assess the evidence for causes working together.
7. Assess whether the result is externally valid for other populations, meaning it holds beyond the people studied.

cards.t: What epidemiology is and the 5 W's
q: what does epidemiology mean
what are the 5 W's of epidemiology
what questions does an epidemiological study ask
cards.x:
Epidemiology is, from the Greek, the science that deals with what falls upon people (epi = upon, demos = people, ology = science). It is a bridge between the biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.

The 5 W's are a mnemonic for the basic questions of any epidemiological study:
- What: the health event or diagnosis.
- Who: the person or population involved.
- Where: the location of the event.
- When: the time period of the event.
- Why: the causes, risk factors and modes of transmission.

cards.t: Where epidemiology has impact (fields it informs)
q: how does epidemiology relate to other fields
what does epidemiology contribute to clinical medicine
why is epidemiology called a bridge between sciences
cards.x:
Epidemiology touches several fields, each for its own reason.
- Public health: the emphasis is on preventing disease.
- Clinical medicine: it helps with disease classification and diagnosis.
- Pathophysiology: it helps us understand the basic biological mechanisms of disease.
- Biostatistics: it quantifies how often disease occurs and how that relates to what came before it, such as exposures.
- Social sciences: it shows the social context in which disease occurs and presents.

That is why it is described as a bridge between the biomedical, social and behavioral sciences.

cards.t: Uses of epidemiologic training
q: what can you do with epidemiologic training
what are the uses of epidemiological training
what is program evaluation in epidemiology
cards.x:
Training in epidemiology prepares you for a set of practical jobs:
- Outbreak response: identifying, reporting and investigating outbreaks in a timely manner.
- Public health surveillance: setting up, managing and evaluating surveillance systems.
- Public health communication: developing and delivering it.
- Disease prioritization: evaluating and ranking diseases of concern, including describing the clinical picture: who gets the disease, who dies from it, and what its outcome is.
- Training and mentoring health professionals.
- Experimental epidemiology: developing a hypothesis for a health concern and designing an experimental model to test it.
- Program evaluation and management: evaluating prevention and intervention programs (for example vaccine and clinical trials) and managing their staff and resources.

cards.t: Founders of epidemiology: Hippocrates, Graunt, Farr, Snow
q: who is the father of field epidemiology
who is the father of modern vital statistics
what did John Graunt do
cards.x:
Counting health and disease goes back centuries, even though epidemiology is a young formal discipline.
- Hippocrates (about 400 years before the common era) explained disease in a rational rather than spiritual way, through environmental and host factors.
- John Graunt (17th century) pioneered tabulating population health and mortality in rates, ratios and proportions, noting differences between males and females, high infant mortality, urban versus rural differences and seasonal variation.
- William Farr (1800s) systematically collected and analyzed Britain's mortality statistics, developed life-table approaches and reported to the authorities and the public. He is the father of modern vital statistics.
- John Snow (mid 1800s), an anesthesiologist, used epidemiologic approaches on the London cholera epidemic. He is the father of field epidemiology, and his studies combine descriptive and analytic work.

cards.t: Epidemiology milestones from the 1800s to today
q: what was the Framingham Heart Study
what did Doll and Hill show
how has epidemiology changed over time
cards.x:
Epidemiology's focus has widened with each era.
- Mid to late 1800s: acute infectious diseases.
- 1930s and 1940s: methods extended to noninfectious diseases, followed after World War II by more research methods and theory, then health outcomes tied to behaviors and attitudes.
- Doll and Hill (1950): smoking and lung cancer.
- Framingham Heart Study (began 1948): a multigenerational study to identify common factors contributing to cardiovascular disease.
- 1960s and 1970s: methods applied to eradicate smallpox worldwide.
- 1980s: studies of injuries and violence.
- 1990s, accelerating after 2001: the deliberate spread of disease, meaning biologic warfare and bioterrorism.
- Continuing: new infectious agents (Ebola virus, human immunodeficiency virus, severe acute respiratory syndrome, COVID (coronavirus disease)) and changed ones (drug-resistant organisms such as tuberculosis, and variations of influenza).

cards.t: Genomic epidemiology
q: what is genomic epidemiology
how does sequencing help an outbreak investigation
how can you tell if cases are part of the same outbreak
cards.x:
Genomic epidemiology means monitoring the genetic makeup of the pathogens that cause disease, which advances in sequencing have made possible. It is one of the most reliable tools in outbreak investigation, and it helps in four ways:
- Early outbreak detection: if the pathogens from different cases are closely related, the cases may be part of the same outbreak.
- Identifying transmission links, meaning a common pathway of spread.
- Identifying or confirming sources of exposure.
- Understanding where disease is and how it is spread out, so cases or outbreaks in different locations can be linked and shown more definitively to be one outbreak.

cards.t: Common sources of epidemiologic data
q: where do epidemiologists get data
what are nonhealth-related data sources
what are examples of epidemiologic data sources
cards.x:
Epidemiologists draw data from four kinds of places:
- Individual persons: questionnaires and surveys, such as in a foodborne illness outbreak, or the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which collects health data on United States residents.
- The environment: samples such as river water or soil, and sensors for environmental changes, for example water from area streams checked for chemical pollutants, or air-quality ratings.
- Health care providers: notifications to the health department when cases of certain diseases are seen, such as reporting cases of meningitis.
- Nonhealth-related sources (financial, legal): sales records and court records, for example cigarette sales or intoxicated-driver arrests.

cards.t: Public health surveillance: what it is and what makes it good
q: what is public health surveillance
what makes a surveillance system effective
why does surveillance need sensitivity and specificity
cards.x:
Public health surveillance is a tool that systematically collects, analyzes and interprets data to help prevent and control disease. It measures what is going on in the population, the need for interventions and the effects of interventions, and it informs decisions. It needs a clear objective that includes how data will be collected, consolidated and analyzed.

Four qualities matter in a surveillance system:
- Timeliness: so effective control measures can be implemented.
- Representation: so it gives an accurate picture of the disease's trend over time.
- Sensitivity: so it identifies individual people with the disease, who can then be treated, quarantined or otherwise controlled.
- Specificity: so it excludes people who do not have the disease.

cards.t: Planning surveillance and case surveillance
q: what is an indicator in surveillance
what is case surveillance
what do you decide when planning surveillance
cards.x:
Before a surveillance system starts, planners settle a list of questions: the health-related event and its case definition, the purpose and objectives, how the data will be used, the legal authority to collect it, who runs it, the data sources and collection method, how often (continuous or intermittent), the population under surveillance, how data are processed, how confidentiality is kept, who analyzes it, and how the information reaches everyone who needs it, including the medical and public health communities and policymakers.

An indicator is a measurable factor used to estimate the size of a health problem and to measure the effects of interventions.

Case surveillance is foundational. Local and state health departments collect data about a person with a disease or condition that poses a serious health threat, such as infectious diseases, foodborne outbreaks and lead poisoning. If the condition is notifiable, it is then reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

cards.t: Types of surveillance: active, passive, sentinel, syndromic
q: what is the difference between active and passive surveillance
what is sentinel surveillance
what is syndromic surveillance
cards.x:
Surveillance types differ in who does the work and how complete the picture is.
- Active: staff regularly contact health care providers for data. It is the most accurate but the most expensive, so it is often used for specific purposes such as during outbreaks or seasonal events.
- Passive: it relies on reports submitted by health care facilities and providers. It is the most common but less comprehensive, data quality is hard to control, and it may lead to under-reporting.
- Sentinel: a prearranged group of reporting sources, normally health care providers, agrees to report all cases of specific conditions. A smaller representative group tracks on behalf of a much larger population and tries to get ahead of an outbreak.
- Syndromic: active or passive, with case definitions based entirely on clinical features (diarrhea instead of cholera, for example). It is the most frequently found system in developing countries.
- Social media is a data source that can be valuable for monitoring disease outbreaks and mental health issues.

cards.t: Uses of surveillance data
k: what surveillance data are used for
q: what is surveillance data used for
how do surveillance data help detect epidemics
why does surveillance matter for antibiotic resistance
cards.x:
Surveillance data are used for many purposes, and they can be sorted by how quickly they are put to use, from quickest to longest-term:

- Acting fast: spotting epidemics, newly emerging health problems, changes in health practices, changes in antibiotic resistance, and changes in the distribution of the population at risk.
- In between: estimating the magnitude of a health problem including its cost, assessing control activities, setting research priorities, determining risk factors, facilitating planning, monitoring risk factors and changes in health practices, and documenting the distribution and spread of disease and injury.
- The longer view: describing the natural history of diseases, facilitating epidemiologic and laboratory research, validating the use of preliminary data, setting research priorities, and documenting the distribution and spread of disease and injury.

cards.t: Reportable (notifiable) diseases
q: what is a reportable disease
which diseases must be reported by telephone
why are diseases made reportable
cards.x:
A reportable (notifiable) disease is one that the law requires to be reported to government authorities. Diseases become reportable because they are of public interest through their contagiousness, severity or frequency. Collecting the data lets authorities monitor the disease and gives early warning of possible outbreaks. In the United States this runs through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System, and a list is produced every year.

How a report is made depends on the disease:
- Mandatory written report: gonorrhea, salmonellosis.
- Mandatory report by telephone: rubeola (measles), pertussis.
- Report of the total number of cases: chickenpox, influenza.
- Cancer: reported to state cancer registries.

"Notifiable" is wide: it covers infections such as botulism, cholera, Lyme disease, syphilis and tuberculosis, resistant organisms, outbreaks themselves, and noninfectious conditions such as elevated blood lead levels, carbon monoxide poisoning and silicosis.

cards.t: Incidence vs prevalence
q: what is the difference between incidence and prevalence
how do I tell incidence from prevalence in a formula
why is prevalence used for chronic disease
cards.x:
Morbidity, the level of disease in a population, is measured by incidence and prevalence.

Incidence is the proportion or rate of people who develop a condition during a particular time period, so its numerator is new cases. Think of it as the speedometer: how fast new cases arrive. Prevalence is the proportion of people who have a condition at or during a time period, so its numerator is all cases present. Think of it as the odometer: how many have accumulated.

Telling them apart in a formula: women in a town reported with heart disease in a health survey, over the number of women residents, is a prevalence; women newly diagnosed in one year, over the women residents at mid-year, is an incidence.

Prevalence is often measured for chronic diseases such as diabetes or osteoarthritis, which last a long time and whose onset is hard to date.

cards.t: Why prevalence depends on duration of illness
q: why can prevalence be high when incidence is low
how does survival affect prevalence
what does low prevalence mean
cards.x:
Prevalence depends on two things: incidence (how many new cases arrive) and duration (how long people stay ill). That is why the two can move apart.

High prevalence may reflect high incidence, prolonged survival without cure, or both. Prolonged survival without cure lengthens the duration, so cases pile up and prevalence rises even if incidence is unchanged.

Low prevalence may mean low incidence, a rapidly fatal process (people die quickly, so few are around to be counted), or rapid recovery.

cards.t: Mortality rates: crude, cause-specific, age-specific, infant, maternal
q: what are the types of mortality rate
what is infant mortality used for
what is the difference between morbidity and mortality
cards.x:
Morbidity and mortality both measure disease burden. Morbidity is having a disease or a symptom of disease; mortality is the death rate, the number of deaths in a group of people at a particular time, which may be given by age, sex or cause.

Common mortality rates:
- Crude: deaths from all causes in a population in a given time period.
- Cause-specific: deaths from a specific cause.
- Age-specific: deaths in a specific age group.
- Infant: infant deaths, used to compare health status between countries. It is a concerning statistic for the United States, which compares poorly with most other developed nations and shows considerable disparities by race and socioeconomic status.
- Maternal: mortality associated with pregnancy.

cards.t: Case fatality rate
q: what is the case fatality rate
why can case fatality rate be wrong early in an outbreak
how is case fatality rate calculated
cards.x:
The case fatality rate is deaths divided by total cases of the disease. So it asks: of the people who got it, how many died?

It can mislead during an outbreak. Early on it may be over-estimated, because the sickest cases are the ones hospitalized and counted. Later it may be under-estimated as testing finds more mild cases, and a long time to resolution can make it look better than it really is.

cards.t: Association vs causation
q: what is the difference between association and causation
what is a risk factor
does epidemiology determine the cause in an individual
cards.x:
Epidemiology does not determine the cause of a disease in one individual. It determines the relationship, or association, between an exposure and how often disease occurs in populations, and we infer causation from association plus other factors.
