An association is an identifiable relationship between an exposure and a disease. It suggests the exposure might cause the disease, and exposures linked with a difference in disease risk are often called risk factors. Most public health interventions are designed on the basis of associations.

Causation implies a true mechanism leading from exposure to disease. Finding an association does not make it causal.

cards.t: Pyramid of associations and the web of causation
q: what is the pyramid of associations
what is the web of causation
why are causes rarely single
cards.x:
The pyramid of associations ranks what an observed link might turn out to be. From the broad base to the narrow top: chance, spurious/artifact, confounded, non-causal, and at the apex causal.

The web of causation explains why a cause is rarely one thing. A cause is an event or condition that plays a role in producing a disease, and most diseases come from an interplay of factors, from an exposure plus additional factors to a whole web: genes, phenotype, microbes, behavior, social organization, environment, the workplace and unknown factors all feeding one disease.

cards.t: Hill's criteria: consistency and strength of association
q: what are Hill's criteria
what does consistency mean for causation
why does a strong association support causation
cards.x:
Hill's criteria are a set of considerations for judging whether an association is likely to be causal; none is a pass-or-fail test on its own. Two of them concern the pattern of the evidence.
- Consistency of findings: the association shows up in multiple studies, across different populations, in differing circumstances and with different study designs.
- Strength of association: a strong association is less likely to be caused by chance or bias. It is one in which the relative risk is either very high or very low.

Most judgments of cause and effect are tentative and open to change with new evidence.

cards.t: Hill's criteria: biological gradient (dose-response)
q: what is dose-response in epidemiology
why is dose-response a good sign of causation
what is the smoking and lung cancer example
cards.x:
The biological gradient, or dose-response, means that changes in exposure go along with a trend in relative risk: more exposure, more risk. It is one of the most reliable indicators of causality.

The classic example is smoking. In each of three studies, the standardized mortality ratio for lung cancer rose with the number of cigarettes smoked per day, with the heaviest smokers (more than 40 a day) far above the lightest (fewer than 10 a day). A steady climb like that is what a dose-response relationship looks like, and it strengthens the case that the exposure causes the disease.

cards.t: Hill's criteria: temporal sequence, plausibility, specificity
q: what is temporal sequence in Hill's criteria
what is biological plausibility
what is specificity of association
cards.x:
The remaining criteria are about logic and biology.
- Temporal sequence: the exposure must come before the disease. In diseases with latency periods it must come before the latent period, and chronic diseases often need long-term exposure.
- Biological plausibility and coherence: the proposed mechanism should make biological sense and must not contradict what is known about the natural history and biology of the disease. But the relationship may be indirect, the data may not yet support the mechanism directly, and existing understanding may need reinterpreting in light of new findings.
- Specificity of association: an exposure leads to a single or characteristic effect, or affects people with a specific susceptibility. Causation is easier to support when associations are specific, but many exposures cause multiple diseases.

cards.t: Endemic, sporadic, epidemic, pandemic
q: what is the difference between endemic, epidemic and pandemic
what does sporadic mean
what is an epidemic
cards.x:
These four words describe how often a disease turns up.
- Endemic: diseases found at chronically low levels in a population.
- Sporadic: diseases that occur at irregular intervals, or as isolated incidents.
- Epidemic: diseases occurring in excess of what might be expected in a population, or an uncontrolled spread in a community.
- Pandemic: world-wide epidemics.

Quick way to separate them: endemic is the steady background level, epidemic is a surge above what is expected, and pandemic is an epidemic that has gone world-wide.

cards.t: Types of epidemics: common source, propagated, mixed
q: what is a common source epidemic
what is the difference between point source and propagated
what is a mixed epidemic
cards.x:
Epidemics are sorted by how people were exposed.
- Common source: a group exposed to the same source. In a point-source epidemic the exposure is brief, within one incubation period. In a continuous one, exposure lasts longer. There is also an intermittent form.
- Propagated: person-to-person transmission.
- Mixed: may start as a common source and then be propagated.
- Other: often zoonotic or vector-borne, for example Lyme disease and West Nile encephalitis.

Quick way to tell common source from propagated: in common source everyone was exposed to the same thing, and in propagated the infection passes along from one person to the next.

cards.t: Reading epidemic curves
q: what does a point source epidemic curve look like
how do I recognize a propagated epidemic on a curve
what is an example of a mixed epidemic
cards.x:
An epidemic curve plots cases by date of onset, and its shape tells you the type of epidemic.
- Point source: one sharp peak, because everyone was exposed at about the same time (within one incubation period). The few late cases are secondary. Example: hepatitis A traced to a food handler.
- Continuous common source: cases keep coming for weeks because the exposure continues, until it is removed. Example: diarrheal illness after water main breaks, ending with the boil-water order and chlorination.
- Propagated: a few scattered cases, then successive, larger peaks as the infection passes person to person. Example: measles.
- Mixed: Shigella at a music festival showed staff cases before the festival, a tall peak among attendees during it, and smaller bars after.

cards.t: R0 vs R (reproduction numbers)
q: what is R0
what is the difference between R0 and R
what is the effective reproduction number
cards.x:
R0 (the basic reproduction number) is the number of cases directly generated by one case in a susceptible population with no interventions. R (the effective reproduction number) is the number of cases generated by one case when interventions or immunity are in place.

So R0 describes how contagious a disease is when nothing is stopping it, and R describes how it is actually behaving once vaccines, prior infection or control measures are at work. Interventions and immunity are what pull R below R0.

cards.t: Immunity and herd immunity
q: what is herd immunity
how does vaccination relate to herd immunity
what is immunity
cards.x:
Immunity is inherited, acquired or induced resistance to infection by a specific pathogen. Acquired resistance after a previous infection comes from protective cellular and antibody responses.

Herd immunity is the cumulative number of immune persons in a population, or the percentage of the population that is immune. It is often discussed in relation to vaccination against a particular pathogen, and it is also affected by natural immunity gained by recovering from the infection. The practical point is that when enough people in a population are immune, the infection has trouble spreading, which also helps protect people who are not immune.

cards.t: Steps of an outbreak investigation
q: what are the steps in an outbreak investigation
what comes first in an outbreak investigation
what are the applications of epidemiology
cards.x:
Epidemiology has five main applications: outbreak investigation, policy development, social and behavioral issues, environmental issues, and occupational health and safety.

An outbreak of a communicable disease is investigated in order:
1. Establish the existence of an outbreak.
2. Prepare for field work.
3. Verify the diagnosis.
4. Define and identify cases.
5. Use descriptive epidemiology to describe and orient the data.
6. Develop a focused hypothesis.
7. Evaluate the hypothesis for validity.
8. Refine the hypothesis as needed.
9. Implement control and prevention methods.
10. Communicate findings: who needs to know, how the information will be communicated, and why.

cards.t: The 1976 Legionnaires' disease outbreak
q: what happened in the 1976 Legionnaires' outbreak
how was the source of Legionnaires' disease found
what study design identified the risk factor
cards.x:
In late July 1976, an epidemic of fatal respiratory disease struck people attending an American Legion convention in Philadelphia, and some non-attendees, some within days of the convention. Doctors with the first cases tried to reach the state health department, but it was closed for the weekend, and deaths had already mounted by Monday. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the state health department then took on the investigation.

Five months after the first cases, a case-control study showed that spending time in the lobby of Hotel A was a risk factor for illness. In December 1976 a laboratory scientist located the source bacteria by continuing to test specimens that had been thought to be dead. Then came control and prevention measures, and communication of the findings.

cards.t: The public health approach: problem to response
k: surveillance risk factor identification intervention evaluation implementation
q: what are the steps of the public health approach
how does public health go from problem to response
cards.x:
The public health approach moves from a problem to a response in four questions, each one answering the next need:
- Surveillance: what is the problem?
- Risk factor identification: what is the cause?
- Intervention evaluation: what works?
- Implementation: how do you do it?

So you first measure the problem, then find what drives it, then test what could fix it, and finally work out how to deliver that fix.

cards.t: Policy development and the policy cycle
q: what are the steps in the policy cycle
what does epidemiology contribute to policy
what is policy built on
cards.x:
Rigorously conducted, reported and communicated epidemiological studies can produce major health policy changes. Policy is built on values, ideology, politics and evidence. Evidence is epidemiology's main contribution; it is not usually the main influence on policy, but it is worth fighting for.

The policy cycle runs in order:
1. Assessment of population health: identify the issue affecting population health.
2. Assessment of potential interventions: identify interventions and provide evidence of their efficacy.
3. Policy choices: made with tools such as computer modeling, then delivered for a consensus decision.
4. Policy implementation: set target goals and allocate the resources.
5. Policy evaluation: collect data on the results of the intervention and plan future modeling.

cards.t: Youth smoking as a policy example
q: how did epidemiology change youth smoking policy
what did the 1994 Surgeon General's report recommend
what measures reduced youth smoking
cards.x:
Youth smoking is the worked example of epidemiology shaping policy. By the 1960s smoking had been linked to multiple health problems, and adult smoking fell by the 1980s, but youth smoking did not.

The 1994 Surgeon General's report recommended moving from campaigns aimed at individual young people to treating youth smoking as a community and population issue. The American Stop Smoking Intervention Study for Cancer Prevention used the epidemiological evidence that secondhand smoke is dangerous to reframe smoking as a societal rather than personal concern.

The measures were eliminating tobacco smoke in public places, less advertising and promotion, less youth access to tobacco, and higher tobacco taxes.

cards.t: Social, environmental and occupational epidemiology
q: what does social and behavioral epidemiology study
what is environmental epidemiology
what is occupational epidemiology
what do occupational epidemiologists do
cards.x:
Social and behavioral epidemiology matters because it helps explain how diseases spread and why health outcomes differ across populations. It looks at how income inequality, poverty, race and discrimination affect health, including access to health care, and at how behavioral risk factors contribute to disease.

Environmental epidemiology studies how environmental factors affect human health, such as exposure to air and water pollution or to hazardous waste disposal sites.

Occupational health epidemiology studies how workers' health is affected by workplace conditions and exposure to hazardous substances. It monitors how often workers are injured or ill, identifies which groups of workers are most affected, determines the reasons, and uses the findings to reduce the risk through regulatory practice.

cards.t: Spirochetes: what they are and the three genera
q: what is a spirochete
how do spirochetes move
what are the three genera of spirochetes
cards.x:
Spirochetes are Gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacteria. They move by endoflagella, which sit inside the cell in the periplasmic space, under the outer membrane. That is why they can swim without any flagella on the outside.

There are three genera: Treponema, Leptospira and Borrelia. Some members are free-living saprobes (organisms that feed on dead or decaying matter) or commensals (harmless passengers) of animals, but each genus also includes disease-causing species, such as the ones behind syphilis, leptospirosis, Lyme disease and relapsing fever.

Most bacteria have circular chromosomes, but these narrow cells may have linear double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid and plasmids, especially Borrelia.

cards.t: Treponema pallidum: the syphilis organism
q: what is Treponema pallidum
how is syphilis transmitted
why can't Treponema pallidum be grown in the lab easily
cards.x:
Treponema pallidum is a thin, regular, coiled bacterium, and humans are its natural hosts. It is a strict parasite with complex growth needs: extremely fastidious and sensitive to its environment, so it cannot survive long outside the human host, and it is difficult to culture because the laboratory needs live host cells to grow it.

It spreads sexually and across the placenta. It binds to epithelial tissue (a mucous membrane or abraded skin), multiplies, then penetrates capillaries, moves into the circulation and multiplies further. Spirochetes appear in lesions and in blood during the first two stages, so syphilis is communicable in the primary and secondary stages.

cards.t: Syphilis: primary, secondary and tertiary disease
q: what are the stages of syphilis
what is a chancre
what happens in tertiary syphilis
cards.x:
Untreated syphilis moves through stages.
- Primary: a hard chancre appears at the site of inoculation. It often heals on its own, so the illness may go undiagnosed.
- Secondary: an upper-respiratory-like illness with fever, headache and sore throat, plus a red or brown rash on the skin, including the palms and soles. The rash often disappears spontaneously.
- Tertiary: can last for many years, with numerous complications in susceptible tissues and organs: neurological and cardiovascular symptoms, and gummas (destructive granulomatous lesions in organs). The Argyll Robertson pupil, an irregular pupil that eventually loses its light reflex, is a tertiary sign.

Because the early signs fade by themselves, a person can feel better while the infection continues.

cards.t: Syphilis stages: incubation, latency and testing at each stage
q: how long does each stage of syphilis last
what is latent syphilis
when is a patient with syphilis most infectious
cards.x:
The stages run in a fixed order, and each has its own findings and tests.
- Incubation: no lesion yet. The treponemes adhere to and penetrate the epithelium, multiply and disseminate, and the person has no symptoms.
- Primary: the chancre appears at the inoculation site, with intense treponemal activity in the body. The chancre later disappears. Dark-field microscopy and serological tests can detect it.
- Primary latency: a healed chancre with little scarring, treponemes in the blood and few if any symptoms. Serological tests are positive.
- Secondary: skin and mucous membrane lesions, hair loss, fever and enlarged lymph nodes. The patient is highly infectious, and symptoms can persist for months. Lesions are tested by dark-field microscopy, and serological tests are positive.
- Latency: a long quiet period in which the treponemes are quiescent unless relapse occurs, and lesions can reappear. The blood test stays positive.
- Tertiary: neural and cardiovascular symptoms and gummas; the treponeme may be shown by deoxyribonucleic acid analysis of tissue.

cards.t: Congenital syphilis
q: what is congenital syphilis
what are snuffles and Hutchinson's teeth
how does a baby get syphilis
cards.x:
Congenital syphilis is syphilis passed from mother to fetus across the placenta (transplacental infection). It shows up as:
- "Snuffles": a nasal discharge after birth.
- Skin eruptions.
- Bone deformation, including Hutchinson's teeth, which are notched incisors caused by the bone and tooth deformation.
- Nervous system abnormalities.

Transplacental spread is one of the two routes of Treponema pallidum, the other being sexual contact.

cards.t: Syphilis testing and treatment
q: how is syphilis diagnosed
what can cause a false-positive rapid plasma reagin
how is syphilis treated
cards.x:
The stages of syphilis can mimic other diseases, so clinicians weigh symptoms, history, microscopy and serology.

Serological tests: the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test detects syphilis antibodies, the VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test is the older version of it, and the fluorescent treponemal antibody-absorption test is another. Dark-field microscopy can examine the chancre and lesions. False-positive rapid plasma reagin results can occur with human immunodeficiency virus infection, Lyme disease, some pneumonias, malaria and lupus.

Penicillin G is the treatment at every stage, with doxycycline as an alternative. Erythromycin and tetracycline are less effective backups for people who cannot take penicillin, for example because of allergy. Current guidance no longer favors erythromycin.

cards.t: Bejel, yaws and pinta (nonsyphilitic treponematoses)
q: what are bejel, yaws and pinta
how do bejel, yaws and pinta differ from syphilis
which organism causes yaws
cards.x:
These three diseases resemble syphilis but are rarely transmitted sexually or congenitally. They are cutaneous and bone diseases endemic to specific regions, usually arid climates and/or countries of the Global South.
- Bejel (sahel): Treponema pallidum subspecies endemicum. A deforming childhood infection of the mouth, nasal cavity, body and hands, found in West Africa and the eastern Mediterranean.
- Yaws: T. pallidum subspecies pertenue. It invades a skin cut, causing a primary ulcer that seeds a second crop of lesions. Found in South America, Africa, Asia and Oceania.
- Pinta: T. carateum. A superficial skin lesion that depigments and scars the skin.

cards.t: Leptospira and leptospirosis
q: what causes leptospirosis
how do people get leptospirosis
who is at risk for leptospirosis
cards.x:
Leptospira are spirochetes with tight, regular coils and a bend or hook at one or both ends. L. biflexa is a harmless, free-living saprobe, while L. interrogans causes leptospirosis, a zoonosis (an animal disease that can spread to people) transmitted mainly through mammal urine.

The bacteria are shed in urine, and infection occurs mainly by contact with contaminated urine, so moisture is required. Those likely to be infected include surfers, water-skiers, veterinarians, farmers and slaughterhouse workers, people who come into contact with infected mammal urine or urine-contaminated water.

It targets the kidneys, liver, brain and eyes. Signs are sudden high fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, conjunctivitis and vomiting, and long-term infection may affect the kidneys and liver.

cards.t: Borrelia hermsii and relapsing fever
q: why does relapsing fever relapse
what causes relapsing fever
how is relapsing fever treated
cards.x:
Borrelia are the arthropod-borne spirochetes: large cells with irregularly spaced coils, passed on by vectors such as ticks. Borrelia hermsii causes relapsing fever. Its reservoirs are mammals such as squirrels, chipmunks and wild rodents, and it is tick-borne.

After an incubation period come high fever, shaking chills, headache and fatigue, nausea, vomiting, muscle aches and abdominal pain. There can be extensive damage to the liver, spleen, heart, kidneys and cranial nerves.

It relapses because the organism changes in the patient's body while the immune system tries to control it. The first antibody response brings the fever down, then a mutant Borrelia with a new antigen escapes that antibody and causes a relapse. Each relapse is a new antigenic form slipping past the last antibody, giving recurrent febrile and afebrile cycles. The most common treatment is tetracycline.

cards.t: Borrelia burgdorferi and the Lyme disease tick cycle
q: what causes Lyme disease
how does the Lyme tick cycle work
why are nymphs important in Lyme disease
cards.x:
Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. It is carried by the white-footed mouse and transmitted by Ixodes ticks in a complex two-year cycle that involves mice and deer.
- Year 1: larval ticks pick up Borrelia from mice.
- Year 2: nymphs, the aggressive feeding stage, bite deer and humans, who are an accidental host. Adults mate on deer, and the eggs start the cycle again.

Humans are outside the normal loop: they are accidental hosts. Predicted Lyme transmission in the United States is concentrated in the Northeast and the upper Midwest.

cards.t: Lyme disease signs, treatment and prevention
q: what is erythema migrans
what are the signs of Lyme disease
how is Lyme disease treated
how do you prevent Lyme disease
cards.x:
Lyme disease is a slowly progressive syndrome that is usually not fatal and mimics neuromuscular and rheumatoid conditions, so it can be mistaken for an autoimmune disorder.

Early signs are a bull's-eye rash at the tick-bite site, called erythema migrans (seen in many but not all patients), along with flu-like fever, headache, stiff neck and dizziness.

If untreated, it can progress to cardiac and neurological symptoms and polyarthritis (inflammation of many joints).

Treatment is tetracycline or amoxicillin.

Prevention: insect repellent containing DEET (diethyltoluamide) is the best prevention, plus checking for ticks. A vaccine for dogs is available. The human vaccine (LYMErix) was withdrawn from the United States market.

cards.t: Curviform bacteria: Vibrio, Campylobacter, Helicobacter
q: how do Vibrio, Campylobacter and Helicobacter differ in shape
which curved bacteria have several flagella
cards.x:
Three genera of curved bacteria are told apart by shape and flagella.
- Vibrio: comma-shaped rods with a single polar flagellum.
- Campylobacter: short spirals or curved rods with one flagellum.
- Helicobacter: tight spirals with several polar flagella.

Quick memory: Vibrio and Campylobacter each have one flagellum, while Helicobacter has several. Helicobacter is a spiral rod, not a spirochete: its flagella sit outside the cell instead of inside it.

cards.t: Vibrio cholerae and cholera
q: how does cholera toxin cause diarrhea
what is the El Tor biotype
how is cholera treated
cards.x:
Vibrio cholerae is comma-shaped, with unique O and H antigens. The El Tor biotype survives longer and is more infectious than other strains. It is ingested in contaminated water, and the infectious dose is large because the vibrios must first pass through the stomach to reach the intestine.

It infects the mucous barrier of the small intestine and is noninvasive. Cholera toxin does the damage. Normally water and electrolytes are absorbed from the intestinal lumen into the blood. With the toxin, the flow reverses: chloride, bicarbonate, sodium, potassium and water pour out into the lumen. The result is secretory diarrhea, the "rice water stool", and the dehydration leads to muscle, circulatory and neurological symptoms.

Treatment is oral rehydration, which replaces the lost water and electrolytes, plus an antibiotic such as tetracycline. A vaccine is available.

cards.t: Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio vulnificus (seafood vibrios)
q: what vibrios come from seafood
who is at risk from Vibrio vulnificus
how is seafood vibrio infection treated
cards.x:
These vibrios are salt-tolerant inhabitants of coastal waters that associate with marine invertebrates.
- Vibrio parahaemolyticus: gastroenteritis from raw seafood, with symptoms similar to cholera.
- Vibrio vulnificus: gastroenteritis from raw oysters, with serious complications in people with diabetes or liver disease. It is one of the "flesh-eating" bacteria, and it is a problem with sewage overflow after hurricanes and other natural disasters.

Many kinds of seafood may carry them, including peak predators (squid, mackerel, tuna), smaller fish (sardines, herring) and filter or bottom feeders (crab, shrimp, oysters, clams), because the pathogens can build up in the food chain.

Fluid and electrolyte replacement is the best treatment; antimicrobial drugs are used occasionally.

cards.t: Campylobacter jejuni and Campylobacter fetus
q: how do Campylobacter jejuni and fetus differ
what does Campylobacter jejuni cause
how do people get Campylobacter
cards.x:
Campylobacter are Gram-negative, slender, curved or spiral rods, often S-shaped or in "gull-winged" pairs, with a single polar flagellum. They are common residents of the intestinal tract, genitourinary tract and oral cavity of birds and mammals. Two species matter.
- C. jejuni: an important cause of bacterial gastroenteritis, spread by food and beverages (water, milk, meat and chicken are common). It reaches the mucosa of the last segment of the small intestine near the colon, burrows through the mucus and multiplies. A heat-labile enterotoxin stimulates a secretory diarrhea like that of cholera, with headache, fever, abdominal pain and bloody or watery diarrhea.
- C. fetus: an opportunist in debilitated people or women late in pregnancy. How humans catch it is uncertain; in veterinary medicine it is a sexually transmitted disease of herd animals. It causes meningitis, pneumonia, arthritis, and septicemia in the newborn.

For the diarrheal illness, treatment is rehydration and electrolyte balance, and antibiotics are rarely needed.

cards.t: Helicobacter pylori and ulcers
q: what does Helicobacter pylori cause
how does H. pylori survive stomach acid
who discovered Helicobacter pylori
cards.x:
Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative, motile, curved bacterium with several polar flagella outside the cell. It is a spiral rod, not a spirochete. The Australian doctors Warren and Marshall discovered it in stomach biopsies from ulcer patients and won a Nobel Prize in Medicine for it.

It causes most stomach and duodenal ulcers and is an apparent cofactor in gastric cancer.

It survives the stomach by making urease, an enzyme that converts urea into ammonium and bicarbonate. Those products raise the local pH around the bacterium, which protects it from the stomach's acid. That same urease is the basis of the rapid urease test: a biopsy is pushed into a gel, the urease's ammonia raises the pH, and the gel changes from negative to positive.

cards.t: Rickettsias: general features
q: what are rickettsias
why can't rickettsias be grown on regular media
how do rickettsias cause damage
cards.x:
Rickettsias are among the smallest bacteria, with a Gram-negative cell wall, and are nonmotile pleomorphic rods or coccobacilli. They are obligate intracellular parasites, so cultivating them requires live cells. Most belong to the genus Rickettsia and cause the illnesses called rickettsioses.

Part of their life cycle is spent in arthropod vectors: ticks, fleas and lice.

They enter endothelial cells (the cells lining blood vessels) and cause necrosis of the vascular lining, producing vasculitis, vascular leakage and thrombosis. This fits the rash and vascular damage seen in these illnesses.

For contrast, the chlamydias are also Gram-negative coccobacilli, while the mycoplasmas are unique among all bacteria in lacking a cell wall and therefore peptidoglycan.

cards.t: Typhus forms (epidemic, endemic) and mite-borne rickettsioses
q: what is the difference between epidemic and endemic typhus
what is Brill-Zinsser disease
what causes scrub typhus
cards.x:
Two typhus forms differ in organism, vector and severity.
- Epidemic typhus: Rickettsia prowazekii, spread by lice (the body louse), with humans as the reservoir. Louse feces are rubbed into the bite, or inhaled. It brings high fever, chills, headache and rash. Brill-Zinsser disease is its recurrent form, in which the illness comes back.
- Endemic (murine) typhus: Rickettsia typhi, spread by fleas and harbored by mice and rats. It is sporadic, in areas of heavy flea infestation, and milder.

Quick way to tell them apart: epidemic typhus goes with lice and humans; endemic typhus goes with fleas and rodents.

Two other rickettsial diseases are mite-borne. Scrub typhus is Orientia tsutsugamushi, carried by the immature mite, with rodents as the reservoir, in Asia, Australia and the Pacific Islands. Rickettsialpox is Rickettsia akari, carried by a mite, with mice as the reservoir, and occurs worldwide.

cards.t: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
q: what causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever
why can Rocky Mountain spotted fever be mistaken for measles
where does Rocky Mountain spotted fever occur
cards.x:
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. It is a zoonosis carried by dog and wood ticks, with small mammals as hosts. The tick passes the organism between dogs and ticks, and through the tick's eggs, and a bite infects a human. Most cases are in the Southeast and the eastern seaboard of the United States.

The endothelial damage shows as a distinct spotted rash, vascular damage, and central nervous system damage up to coma. It may also damage the heart. Early on the rash may be misdiagnosed as measles, a viral disease with very different treatment.

cards.t: Ehrlichia and human monocytic ehrlichiosis
q: what causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis
how is ehrlichiosis transmitted
cards.x:
Human monocytic ehrlichiosis is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, and it is spread by tick bite. Ehrlichia are tick-borne members of the rickettsia group.

Like Rocky Mountain spotted fever, then, it is a tick-borne rickettsial disease, but it has its own organism: Ehrlichia chaffeensis here, Rickettsia rickettsii there.

cards.t: The Weil-Felix test
q: what is the Weil-Felix test based on
what is the story of the Weil-Felix test in World War II
cards.x:
The Weil-Felix test rests on a cross-reaction between Proteus bacteria and Rickettsia prowazekii, the cause of epidemic typhus. A cross-reaction means that antibodies made against one organism also react with the other, so Proteus can stand in for the rickettsia in the test.

It has a famous history. During World War II two Polish doctors used it to make the occupying Germans, who feared typhus outbreaks, avoid towns in southeastern Poland.

cards.t: Coxiella burnetii and Q fever
q: what causes Q fever
how do people catch Q fever
who should get the Q fever vaccine
cards.x:
Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, an intracellular parasite. The Q stands for "query", meaning unknown; historic cases most likely arose from contaminated milking barns.

Coxiella is harbored by a wide range of vertebrates and arthropods. Infectious material includes urine, feces, milk and airborne particles, and it is usually inhaled, causing pneumonitis (lung inflammation), fever and inflammation of the liver.

Tetracycline is the treatment. A vaccine is available for those at highest risk: veterinarians, farmers and laboratory technicians.

cards.t: Bartonella: trench fever, cat-scratch disease, bacillary angiomatosis
q: what diseases does Bartonella cause
how do people get cat-scratch disease
how is Bartonella treated
cards.x:
Bartonella is a small, Gram-negative, fastidious bacterium that is cultured on blood agar. It causes three illnesses:
- Trench fever, spread by lice.
- Cat-scratch disease, a lymphatic infection after a clawing injury by a cat.
- Bacillary angiomatosis, in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.

Treatment is tetracycline, erythromycin or rifampin.

cards.t: Tetracycline: the recurring drug for these bacteria
k: which drug treats relapsing fever Lyme cholera
q: which infections are treated with tetracycline
how does tetracycline work
what is tetracycline used for in miscellaneous bacterial infections
cards.x:
Tetracycline is a very broad-spectrum antibiotic that targets prokaryotic ribosomes, at the 30S subunit. It keeps turning up as a treatment option across this group of bacteria:
- Relapsing fever (Borrelia): the most common option.
- Lyme disease: tetracycline or amoxicillin.
- Cholera: oral rehydration and tetracycline.
- Q fever (Coxiella).
- Bartonella: tetracycline, erythromycin or rifampin.
- Mycoplasma: tetracycline or erythromycin.

For syphilis, penicillin G is the first choice; tetracycline is a less effective backup for people who cannot take penicillin.

cards.t: The chlamydial life cycle: elementary and reticulate bodies
q: what is the difference between an elementary body and a reticulate body
how does Chlamydia replicate
why can't Chlamydia make its own energy
cards.x:
The Chlamydiaceae are obligate intracellular parasites: small cells with a Gram-negative cell wall that alternate between two stages.
- Elementary body: small, metabolically inactive, extracellular and infectious. It is the form released by the infected host cell.
- Reticulate body: noninfectious and actively dividing. It grows inside host-cell vacuoles but cannot make its own adenosine triphosphate.

The cycle: elementary bodies attach and are taken into a phagosome (a membrane-bound sac inside the host cell), turn into reticulate bodies that divide by binary fission, become elementary bodies again, and are released to infect new cells. Remember: elementary is the infectious traveler, reticulate is the dividing worker.

cards.t: Chlamydia trachomatis: trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis
q: what is trachoma
how do babies get inclusion conjunctivitis
what are the strains of Chlamydia trachomatis
cards.x:
Chlamydia trachomatis has a human reservoir and two strains: trachoma and lymphogranuloma venereum. The trachoma strain attacks the mucous membranes of the eyes, genitourinary tract and lungs.

- Ocular trachoma is severe, deforms the eyelid and cornea, and may cause blindness. It affects people in tropical climates with poor sanitation, flying insects and poor hygiene.
- Inclusion conjunctivitis is acquired by a baby as it passes through the birth canal, and it is prevented by prophylaxis.

cards.t: Chlamydia trachomatis: genital infection and lymphogranuloma venereum
q: what problems does genital chlamydia cause
what is lymphogranuloma venereum
how is chlamydia diagnosed in lymphogranuloma venereum
cards.x:
As a sexually transmitted infection, Chlamydia trachomatis has been the first or second most prevalent in the United States in recent years. It causes urethritis, cervicitis and salpingitis (inflammation of the fallopian tubes, part of pelvic inflammatory disease), with infertility and scarring as the lasting damage.

Lymphogranuloma venereum, from the other strain, is a disfiguring disease of the external genitalia and pelvic lymphatics. Diagnosis can show an inclusion body next to the nucleus of an infected cell.

cards.t: Chlamydophila pneumoniae and psittaci
q: what is Chlamydophila
what is ornithosis
what does Chlamydophila pneumoniae cause
cards.x:
Chlamydophila is a new genus made up of former Chlamydia members.
- C. pneumoniae: an atypical pneumonia, serious in asthma patients.
- C. psittaci: ornithosis, a zoonosis transmitted to humans from birds ("ornith" means bird) and highly communicable among birds. It causes pneumonia or a flu-like infection with fever and lung congestion.

Some current sources have folded these two back into the genus Chlamydia (Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia psittaci), so you may see either name.

cards.t: Mycoplasmas (cell-wall-deficient bacteria)
q: why don't mycoplasmas respond to penicillin
what does Mycoplasma pneumoniae cause
what are mollicutes
cards.x:
Mycoplasmas, the mollicutes, are bacteria that naturally lack cell walls, so they are highly pleomorphic (their shapes vary widely). They require special lipids from host membranes.

Treatment is tetracycline or erythromycin, but not penicillin: penicillin acts on the cell wall, and with no peptidoglycan present it has nothing to act on.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes primary atypical pneumonia: the pathogen spreads slowly over the interior respiratory surfaces, causing fever, chest pain and sore throat. M. genitalium and Ureaplasma urealyticum are weak sexually transmitted pathogens.

cards.t: Dental caries and plaque
q: how do cavities form
what bacteria cause dental caries
what is plaque
cards.x:
Dental caries (cavities) is a slow, progressive infection of irregular areas of the enamel surface, and the most commonly diagnosed of all human diseases. The mouth is a complex, dynamic ecosystem of hundreds of microbial species.

It begins when slime-forming Streptococcus species colonize the tooth, with Actinomyces cross-adhering in the biofilm. Streptococcus mutans is commonly found. This forms plaque, a thick, adherent layer harboring masses of bacteria whose acid dissolves enamel. Mature biofilms are polymicrobial. Plaque left on and between teeth brings secondary invaders such as Lactobacillus, Bacteroides and Fusobacterium.

cards.t: Periodontal disease: calculus, gingivitis, periodontitis
q: what causes gingivitis
how does periodontal disease differ from caries
what is calculus
cards.x:
Periodontal disease is a soft-tissue disease, and it takes a different road from caries once plaque has built up.
- Caries branch: acidification and cavitation lead to caries and tooth destruction.
- Calculus branch: plaque calcifies into calculus (tartar) above and below the gingiva and irritates it, causing gingivitis. The pockets between tooth and gingiva are then invaded by spirochetes and Gram-negative bacilli. The tooth socket may become involved (periodontitis), with bone resorption, and the tooth may be lost.

Quick way to tell them apart: acid from plaque harms the hard enamel, while calculus irritates the gums.

cards.t: How each miscellaneous bacterium is transmitted
q: how is Treponema pallidum transmitted
which of these bacteria are tick-borne
which are spread by lice or fleas
cards.x:
A quick map of how each is spread:
- Treponema pallidum: sexual contact and transplacental; humans are the only natural host. Bejel, yaws and pinta are rarely sexual or congenital and are endemic in particular regions.
- Leptospira interrogans: contact with mammal urine in moist settings.
- Borrelia hermsii: tick bite, with rodent reservoirs. Borrelia burgdorferi: Ixodes tick bite, white-footed mouse reservoir, deer in the cycle, and humans as accidental hosts.
- Vibrio cholerae: ingested in contaminated water. Other seafood vibrios: raw seafood.
- Campylobacter jejuni: food and beverages. C. fetus: uncertain in humans.
- Rickettsia prowazekii: lice. R. typhi: fleas. R. rickettsii: dog and wood ticks. Ehrlichia: ticks.
- Coxiella burnetii: usually inhaled. Bartonella: lice (trench fever) or a cat's scratch.
- Chlamydia trachomatis: sexual contact or passage through the birth canal. Chlamydophila psittaci: birds.
- Mycoplasma genitalium and Ureaplasma urealyticum: sexual contact.

cards.t: Coxiella's resistant spore-like form
q: does Coxiella form endospores
why is Coxiella so hardy
cards.x:
Coxiella is unusually hardy, but its resistance does not come from a true endospore like those of Bacillus and Clostridium. Current texts describe a resistant, spore-like small-cell form instead.

So the toughness of Coxiella comes from that resistant small-cell form, and the contrast to remember is with Bacillus and Clostridium, which make true endospores.

cards.t: Human granulocytic anaplasmosis (formerly granulocytic ehrlichiosis)
q: what is human granulocytic anaplasmosis
what is the new name for human granulocytic ehrlichiosis
what organism causes anaplasmosis
cards.x: Human granulocytic ehrlichiosis is now called human granulocytic anaplasmosis. It is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum. It is tick-borne, like human monocytic ehrlichiosis, which is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis. So if you meet the older name, granulocytic ehrlichiosis, it is the same disease as anaplasmosis.
